questions.topic: ACS diagnosis and myocardial infarction classification
questions.question: A patient with systemic illness has a clear rise and fall in high-sensitivity troponin, with at least one value above the assay’s sex-specific 99th percentile. No ischemic or acute coronary evidence is established yet. What is the best-supported current label?
options: Acute myocardial injury
Primary myocardial infarction
Secondary myocardial infarction
Chronic myocardial injury
questions.explanation:
Acute Injury Requires a Mechanistic Diagnosis

Correct answer: Acute myocardial injury

Establish the Biomarker Pattern First

**A rise and/or fall with a value above the sex-specific 99th percentile supports acute myocardial injury.** Use the actual assay and sampling context.

The supported label should precede any more specific mechanism assignment. An acute illness can coexist with coronary disease, so neither automatic infarction labeling nor automatic dismissal is appropriate.

A laboratory boundary does not independently determine the next procedure or antithrombotic prescription.

Connect Further Assessment to the Clinical Question

**Evaluate symptoms, ECG, hemodynamics and appropriate imaging.** The urgency depends on the evolving presentation, including whether an acute coronary process is plausible.

Treat the underlying illness and instability while clarifying cardiac involvement. Consider whether additional testing will change care and whether its procedural burden is acceptable.

Record the measured values, time course and relevant clinical findings rather than relying on a nonspecific positive-troponin description. If evidence changes, revise the diagnosis transparently. A nonspecific injury label does not mean the finding is harmless, and a more specific infarction label should not be used merely to make the record appear decisive. Communication should separate what is established from what remains under evaluation so subsequent clinicians do not inherit an unsupported assumption about coronary thrombosis.

Primary myocardial infarction: Primary infarction requires an appropriate spontaneous ischemic or acute coronary presentation; the troponin pattern alone does not establish that mechanism.

Secondary myocardial infarction: Another acute illness can produce secondary infarction, but a trigger and acute injury alone are insufficient; establish ischemia and the required supporting assessment.

Chronic myocardial injury: Chronic injury is an elevated persistent pattern rather than the clear acute rise and fall supplied in this question.

Joint ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF Fifth Universal Definition of MI, 2026 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13523810/

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: A patient develops spontaneous ischemic chest pain, dynamic ischemic ECG changes and acute troponin elevation. Angiography identifies spontaneous coronary artery dissection as the culprit, without a preceding cardiac procedure or an alternative acute illness. Under the 2026 clinical classification, which category applies?
options: Primary myocardial infarction
Secondary myocardial infarction
Procedure-related myocardial infarction
Acute nonischemic myocardial injury
questions.explanation:
Primary MI Includes Acute Coronary Pathologies Beyond Atherothrombosis

Correct answer: Primary myocardial infarction

Classify the Clinical Setting and Then the Cause

**The 2026 primary category includes spontaneous acute coronary pathology**, not only plaque-associated thrombosis. The identified SCAD mechanism fits that setting.

Keep the clinical category, ECG presentation and coronary etiology distinct. A category name does not by itself determine whether PCI is beneficial for the specific culprit process.

Historical type numbering may appear in older trials and examination sources; label its year rather than assuming a one-to-one translation without reviewing the mechanism.

Avoid Classification Errors Created by the Investigation

**A diagnostic procedure does not retroactively become the cause of an event that preceded it.** Establish the temporal sequence clearly.

Review symptoms, biomarker timing and imaging together. Document the culprit mechanism when demonstrated instead of stopping at an undifferentiated MI label.

Care remains guided by hemodynamic stability, ongoing ischemia and the specific coronary pathology. In a patient with SCAD, a standard plaque-rupture intervention strategy should not be adopted simply because both events fall under a broad primary category. Explain the diagnosis and its implications using the actual findings. The reason for specificity is to guide a suitable treatment and follow-up plan, not to replace immediate stabilization with a terminology exercise.

Secondary myocardial infarction: Secondary infarction is considered when another acute condition creates the supply–demand mismatch; here the presentation arises from a primary acute coronary pathology itself.

Procedure-related myocardial infarction: This category concerns infarction complicating a cardiac procedure in the applicable time frame; angiography performed to diagnose an already-present spontaneous event does not make it procedure-related.

Acute nonischemic myocardial injury: The case supplies ischemic findings and a culprit acute coronary pathology, so a nonischemic injury label fails to account for the demonstrated mechanism.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: During severe anemia, a patient develops ischemic discomfort, new ST depression and an acute troponin rise. Imaging shows a new regional abnormality in an ischemic distribution. Coronary assessment identifies obstructive CAD without an acute culprit pathology. Under the 2026 definition, which diagnosis is supported?
options: Chronic myocardial injury with incidental CAD
Primary myocardial infarction
Acute myocardial injury without established infarction
Secondary myocardial infarction
questions.explanation:
Secondary MI Requires More Than a Supply–Demand Trigger

Correct answer: Secondary myocardial infarction

Confirm the Ischemic Mechanism

**The 2026 secondary category addresses infarction triggered by another acute condition causing supply–demand mismatch.** The stated anemia is the trigger, not proof by itself.

Here, ischemic evidence and the objective assessment support the diagnosis. If an acute coronary culprit had instead been found, primary MI would need consideration.

The presence of an illness should therefore neither automatically create nor automatically exclude an infarction diagnosis.

Treat the Trigger and the Demonstrated Substrate

**Correct the anemia and assess ongoing ischemia and hemodynamic stability.** Investigate and control its cause, including bleeding when relevant.

Subsequent coronary and ventricular treatment follows the demonstrated disease and the individual benefit–risk balance rather than a reflex plaque-rupture regimen.

Document which findings confirmed infarction and which condition triggered it. When additional imaging is not feasible or appropriate, communicate the limits of diagnostic certainty rather than implying that every necessary test was performed. A historical type-2 label may appear in older literature, but its use should be dated because the current confirmation framework is more specific. The classification helps distinguish the treatment problem: managing an acute trigger and clinically important coronary substrate differs from assuming a new coronary thrombosis solely from an elevated troponin.

Chronic myocardial injury with incidental CAD: A clear acute troponin change, new ischemic ECG findings and a new regional abnormality do not fit an unchanged chronic injury pattern.

Primary myocardial infarction: Primary MI remains an important alternative during acute illness, but this case establishes a mismatch trigger and obstructive disease without an acute coronary culprit.

Acute myocardial injury without established infarction: That label is appropriate while infarction remains unconfirmed, but the stem adds ischemic findings and the objective features supporting secondary MI.

Joint ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF Fifth Universal Definition of MI, 2026 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13523810/

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: Five days after elective PCI, a patient develops acute chest pain, new ischemic ECG changes and a new troponin rise. Angiography shows thrombosis of the recently treated segment, and echo shows a corresponding new regional wall-motion abnormality. Under the 2026 clinical classification, which category applies?
options: Procedure-related myocardial infarction
Primary myocardial infarction unrelated to the recent procedure
Secondary myocardial infarction from a systemic demand trigger
Expected post-PCI myocardial injury without infarction
questions.explanation:
Procedure-Related MI Within the 2026 Time Window

Correct answer: Procedure-related myocardial infarction

Use the Clinical Time Window and Causal Evidence

**The 2026 definition applies a 30-day window to infarction caused by a cardiac procedural complication.** The diagnosis is not established merely because troponin is elevated after a procedure.

Confirmation requires a demonstrated coronary complication or new ischemic regional dysfunction/loss of viable myocardium. Both are required when the complication occurs during the procedure or the procedure is performed in acute MI. This day-five case supplies both, beyond an expected biomarker leak.

The framework differs from older PCI/CABG-specific type numbering and should be identified by year when teaching or comparing studies.

Preserve the Sequence of Events

**Distinguish a complication of treatment from the original condition that prompted treatment.** Baseline biomarkers, intervening recovery and the new episode matter.

Review antiplatelet exposure, adherence, procedural findings and other contributors while arranging urgent management of the demonstrated complication.

Immediately after a procedure, the 2026 framework describes a likely diagnosis when biomarkers increase from baseline and continue rising at six hours after intervention, for example above five times URL, or at twenty-four hours after surgery, for example above thirty-five times URL. These are context-dependent examples supporting suspicion, not standalone confirmation thresholds. Apply the coronary and ventricular confirmation requirements as well. This differs from importing historical PCI/CABG type-number thresholds into the new framework. Record the culprit, timing and regional consequence while treating recurrent occlusion urgently.

Primary myocardial infarction unrelated to the recent procedure: The 2026 framework places an infarction caused by a coronary complication within 30 days of a cardiac procedure in the procedure-related category; the documented early stent event fits that context.

Secondary myocardial infarction from a systemic demand trigger: No alternative systemic mismatch trigger explains the event; angiography instead identifies a coronary complication of the recent intervention.

Expected post-PCI myocardial injury without infarction: Routine injury after an intervention does not explain this new ischemic episode with a demonstrated coronary complication and corresponding new ventricular abnormality.

Joint ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF Fifth Universal Definition of MI, 2026 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13523810/

ESC official Fifth Universal Definition diagnostic slides, 2026 — https://dam-assets.escardio.org/download/b2e827b89baa11f1879e62eac143aa37

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: A stable patient presents 45 minutes after ischemic-sounding chest pain began. The ECG has no persistent ST elevation. Initial hs-cTn is below the 99th percentile but does not meet a validated assay-specific very-low rule-out threshold. Which next approach is appropriate?
options: Use the validated assay-specific serial pathway with repeat ECG and clinical reassessment
Exclude MI because the initial value is below the 99th percentile
Apply a numeric rule-out cutoff from a different hs-cTn assay
Diagnose unstable angina immediately from the normal first sample
questions.explanation:
Serial High-Sensitivity Troponin in an Early Presenter

Correct answer: Use the validated assay-specific serial pathway with repeat ECG and clinical reassessment

Use the Correct Algorithm for the Actual Assay

**Validated 0/1-hour or 0/2-hour pathways combine baseline concentration and change**, together with the clinical and ECG findings.

The zero time refers to the initial sample. A very early presentation and a value below the 99th percentile do not automatically satisfy a single-sample discharge rule.

Use the laboratory’s validated assay-specific concentrations and deltas rather than a universal number.

Preserve Clinical Reassessment

**Repeat assessment when pain persists, recurs or the clinical picture changes.** A biomarker pathway does not override an indication for immediate invasive evaluation.

An observation-zone result requires further assessment rather than forced assignment to rule-in or rule-out. Consider repeat sampling and targeted testing according to risk.

Describe the actual time course so later clinicians can distinguish an early nondiagnostic sample from a completed negative pathway. Rule-out of infarction does not exclude every cause of ischemic symptoms or every dangerous alternative diagnosis. Similarly, a rule-in biomarker pattern identifies a high-probability injury presentation that still requires clinical interpretation of the cause. The aim is a validated diagnostic sequence, with disposition based on the integrated evidence rather than one apparently reassuring laboratory result.

Exclude MI because the initial value is below the 99th percentile: The diagnostic injury boundary is not itself a single-sample early rule-out criterion; troponin can still rise after a very recent symptom onset.

Apply a numeric rule-out cutoff from a different hs-cTn assay: Different assays have different validated concentrations and change thresholds; a cutoff cannot be transferred merely because both tests are called high sensitivity.

Diagnose unstable angina immediately from the normal first sample: Unstable angina remains possible, but an early first sample cannot establish the absence of evolving injury; complete the appropriate serial assessment.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

ACC emergency chest-pain evaluation consensus pathway, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2022.08.750

questions.question: A patient has recurrent rest discomfort with transient ischemic ST depression. Appropriately timed serial hs-cTn values remain below the assay’s injury threshold without a significant rise. The ischemic presentation remains clinically convincing. Which diagnosis is most appropriate?
options: Chronic stable angina
NSTEMI established by the dynamic ECG alone
Unstable angina
Nonischemic chest pain established by the negative troponins
questions.explanation:
Unstable Angina After Adequate Serial Testing

Correct answer: Unstable angina

Separate Ischemia From Demonstrable Injury

**Unstable angina describes an unstable ischemic presentation without established acute myocardial injury.** Sensitive assays have reclassified many older unstable-angina cases as infarction.

That change in frequency does not eliminate unstable angina. Adequate timing and serial testing matter before using the label.

The early single negative sample in a new presentation is a different scenario from the completed assessment stated here.

Manage the Risk Rather Than the Biomarker Label Alone

**Persistent or recurrent ischemia and instability influence the urgency of care.** A negative troponin does not justify dismissal of dynamic ischemic findings.

Review the ECG during and after symptoms, assess hemodynamics and investigate according to the ACS risk pathway. Alternative causes of symptoms and ST changes must also be considered.

questions.question: A patient has acute troponin elevation and a possible ischemic presentation. Angiography shows no stenosis ≥50%, and no mechanism has been established. Under the 2026 definition, which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Assign coronary vasospasm as the mechanism and start a definitive vasospasm regimen
Assign myocarditis as the final diagnosis and arrange follow-up echocardiography
Treat MINOCA as a myocardial-injury working diagnosis and investigate the cause, including appropriately timed CMR
Assign occult plaque disruption and prescribe a fixed long-term ACS regimen
questions.explanation:
MINOCA Is a Working Diagnosis Requiring Further Evaluation

Correct answer: Treat MINOCA as a myocardial-injury working diagnosis and investigate the cause, including appropriately timed CMR

Use the Updated Working Terminology

**The Fifth Universal Definition expands MINOCA as myocardial injury with nonobstructive coronary arteries.** Its purpose is to preserve diagnostic uncertainty until the mechanism is established.

The term is not a final confirmation of infarction and does not mean that angiography has proved normal coronary physiology.

Label older infarction-based terminology by year when interpreting historical trials and guidelines.

Select Tests That Can Establish the Cause

**CMR can distinguish ischemic from several nonischemic injury patterns.** The 2026 document favors early assessment, ideally within two weeks when feasible.

Intravascular imaging or coronary functional testing can address selected unresolved coronary mechanisms. Review noncardiac causes when the presentation warrants them.

Select testing to resolve the actual differential and change treatment. An ischemic scar pattern supports infarction but does not independently identify plaque disruption, embolism or spasm. A normal study does not establish a specific coronary mechanism or exclude every small or transient injury. Interpret tissue characterization alongside symptom timing, ECG and coronary findings. The 2026 CMR consensus describes myocarditis assessment using both an edema-sensitive T2 marker and an injury-sensitive T1 marker; late enhancement alone is not the complete framework.

CMR finding | Interpretation | Limitation

Subendocardial or transmural LGE in a coronary territory | Ischemic injury pattern | Does not establish the coronary mechanism

Subepicardial or midwall LGE with edema | Supports a nonischemic inflammatory process | Integrate T1/T2 markers and clinical findings

No diagnostic scar or edema pattern | No tissue mechanism established by this scan | Timing and lesion size affect sensitivity

Assign coronary vasospasm as the mechanism and start a definitive vasospasm regimen: Vasospasm is a genuine coronary alternative, but nonobstructive anatomy does not demonstrate it; targeted functional evaluation may be needed after other causes are assessed.

Assign myocarditis as the final diagnosis and arrange follow-up echocardiography: Myocarditis is a plausible cause of injury with nonobstructive coronaries, but the angiogram alone cannot establish it; tissue characterization and the clinical differential remain necessary.

Assign occult plaque disruption and prescribe a fixed long-term ACS regimen: Plaque disruption can be missed on angiography and may warrant selected intravascular imaging, but the working label alone does not establish this mechanism or its definitive treatment.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

EACVI/ESC clinical consensus on CMR implementation, 2026 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag678

questions.question: A hemodynamically stable patient has abrupt severe chest pain maximal at onset, an interarm pulse difference and a new diastolic murmur. ECG shows ischemic changes. Which investigation should be prioritized before committing to an antithrombotic or fibrinolytic ACS pathway?
options: Immediate coronary-only angiography without assessing the aorta
Serial troponin testing as the principal discriminator
D-dimer as a stand-alone exclusion test
Urgent CT angiography directed at suspected acute aortic syndrome
questions.explanation:
Acute Aortic Syndrome Can Present With Myocardial Ischemia

Correct answer: Urgent CT angiography directed at suspected acute aortic syndrome

Recognize the Competing Emergency

**Acute aortic disease can cause coronary malperfusion and ischemic ECG changes.** Those findings do not establish primary coronary atherothrombosis as the cause.

Abrupt maximal pain, pulse or pressure differences and a new aortic regurgitation murmur raise concern in the stated presentation.

A normal chest radiograph would not adequately exclude the diagnosis.

Match Imaging to Stability and Availability

**CT is recommended as initial diagnostic imaging for suspected acute aortic syndrome in suitable patients.** TEE or MRI can be alternatives according to circumstances.

If instability makes transport unsafe, bedside assessment and specialist coordination may favor another rapid imaging route. Begin appropriate monitoring and urgent aortic-team involvement.

Fibrinolysis or indiscriminate anticoagulation can be dangerous when dissection is the actual mechanism, so resolve this specific high-risk differential promptly rather than waiting for a complete biomarker series. This is not a reason to delay reperfusion in every typical coronary presentation; the stem supplies substantial aortic red flags. Document the reasoning and proceed rapidly with definitive care once the anatomy is known. The purpose of recognizing the mimic is to choose the correct emergency pathway, not simply add another diagnosis to a list.

Immediate coronary-only angiography without assessing the aorta: Coronary assessment may become necessary, but the abrupt pain, pulse discrepancy and new regurgitant murmur require urgent evaluation of the suspected aortic emergency.

Serial troponin testing as the principal discriminator: Troponin can identify myocardial injury but cannot exclude aortic dissection or establish whether coronary ischemia is due to aortic involvement.

D-dimer as a stand-alone exclusion test: A low D-dimer can contribute in selected low-probability pathways, but this high-risk presentation requires definitive imaging rather than biomarker exclusion alone.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man with ongoing ischemic chest discomfort has new J-point elevation confined to V2 and V3, without LVH or bundle branch block. Which minimum elevation in both leads meets the standard age- and sex-specific threshold?
options: 2.0 mm
1.0 mm
1.5 mm
2.5 mm
questions.explanation:
Lead-Specific ST-Elevation Thresholds

Correct answer: 2.5 mm

Apply the Correct Lead and Patient Category

**In V2–V3, men younger than forty require at least 2.5 mm**, compared with 2 mm in older men and 1.5 mm in women.

Use the J-point and contiguous leads. The ordinary 1-mm threshold for other leads must not replace the V2–V3 qualification.

The standard framework assumes the absence of confounding LVH or bundle branch block, as specified in this stem.

Use the ECG to Direct Timely Clinical Assessment

**Thresholds support a working reperfusion diagnosis in the appropriate presentation**, not a complete etiologic diagnosis from voltage alone.

Evaluate symptom timing, prior tracings and reciprocal or evolving changes. Some acute occlusions do not display conventional qualifying elevation, and some nonischemic conditions do.

Do not wait for biomarkers to become positive when the presentation warrants emergency reperfusion assessment. Conversely, an isolated voltage criterion should be interpreted with its clinical context and the possibility of repolarization variants or other causes. Correct electrode placement and calibration matter when measurements sit near a boundary. The teaching point is a precise standard criterion, while the bedside decision remains an integrated assessment of possible acute coronary occlusion.

Lead group | Standard J-point threshold

V2–V3, men <40 years | ≥2.5 mm

V2–V3, men ≥40 years | ≥2.0 mm

V2–V3, women | ≥1.5 mm

Other standard leads | ≥1 mm in the required contiguous distribution

2.0 mm: Two millimeters is the V2–V3 threshold for men aged forty or older; the stated patient is thirty-five.

1.0 mm: One millimeter is the standard threshold in other qualifying leads, but V2–V3 require the specified age- and sex-specific threshold.

1.5 mm: One and a half millimeters is the V2–V3 threshold for women, not a man younger than forty.

Joint ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF Fifth Universal Definition of MI, 2026 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13523810/

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A patient with ongoing ischemic discomfort has horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with prominent anterior R waves. No conventional ST-elevation territory is apparent. Which additional lead set most directly evaluates the suspected missed infarct?
options: Repeat limb leads with emphasis on aVR
Right-sided leads V3R–V4R
Posterior leads V7–V9
Repeat standard V1–V3 after moving them superiorly
questions.explanation:
Posterior Infarction Hidden in Anterior Reciprocal Changes

Correct answer: Posterior leads V7–V9

Interpret the Reciprocal View

**Posterior injury may appear as ST depression in anterior leads**, often with a prominent R wave as the reciprocal counterpart of a posterior Q-wave pattern.

Posterior V7–V9 recordings directly sample the suspected territory. The ESC 2023 supplementary ECG framework identifies elevation of at least 0.5 mm in V7–V9 as supporting posterior STEMI in the compatible clinical setting; standard anterior-lead thresholds should not be substituted for this posterior criterion.

Prominent anterior R waves have other causes, so the acute symptoms and ST pattern are necessary context rather than proof from R-wave height alone.

Act on the Integrated Occlusion Assessment

**A standard twelve-lead ECG can miss a posterior elevation pattern.** Additional leads should be acquired promptly while urgent coronary assessment proceeds.

Posterior infarction may accompany inferior or lateral involvement; do not force an isolated territory when the full tracing shows more extensive injury.

Serial ECGs, symptoms and hemodynamics remain important. A nondiagnostic initial biomarker does not remove concern during an early ongoing ischemic presentation. Distinguish this pattern from diffuse subendocardial ischemia and other causes of anterior depression using the full ECG and clinical evidence. Record electrode placement and acquisition time so the posterior tracing can be compared correctly. The useful next test is the lead set that resolves the suspected blind spot, not a delay for unrelated investigations.

Repeat limb leads with emphasis on aVR: Limb leads can clarify other ischemic patterns, but the described anterior reciprocal changes specifically call for posterior recording rather than aVR-focused assessment.

Right-sided leads V3R–V4R: Right-sided leads assess RV involvement, particularly with inferior infarction; they do not directly test the posterior territory suggested by anterior reciprocal depression.

Repeat standard V1–V3 after moving them superiorly: High right-precordial placement has other uses, but does not substitute for posterior leads in evaluating the suspected posterior injury pattern.

questions.question: A patient with inferior ST elevation develops hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure and relatively clear lungs. Which additional ECG recording most directly evaluates the suspected accompanying chamber involvement?
options: Repeat standard V5 and V6 at the same positions
Posterior leads V7–V9
Right precordial leads V3R and V4R
High right-precordial V1 and V2 recordings
questions.explanation:
Right Ventricular Involvement in Inferior Infarction

Correct answer: Right precordial leads V3R and V4R

Localize the Hemodynamic Problem

**Inferior infarction can involve the RV**, producing impaired forward delivery, venous congestion and hypotension without prominent pulmonary edema.

ESC guidance recommends right precordial recording in suspected inferior STEMI. Elevation in V3R–V4R supports ongoing RV ischemia.

**Avoid reflex preload reduction in a hypotensive patient with suspected RV involvement.** Evaluate nitrate exposure, filling, rhythm and perfusion before treatment.

Fluid may help selected underfilled patients but should be titrated with reassessment; indiscriminate large-volume loading can worsen RV dilation and congestion.

Record right-sided leads promptly because changes can evolve. The purpose of the additional tracing is to clarify a management-relevant extension of the infarct, not delay definitive care while seeking a perfect localization label.

Repeat standard V5 and V6 at the same positions: Lateral leads may show additional infarct extension, but do not replace right-sided leads for evaluating the suspected RV territory.

Posterior leads V7–V9: Posterior leads evaluate posterior injury and are useful with compatible reciprocal changes, but the hemodynamic pattern here specifically raises concern for RV involvement.

questions.question: A patient with established LBBB has persistent ischemic discomfort. A predominantly negative QRS lead has an S-wave depth of 8 mm and discordant J-point elevation of 3 mm. Which interpretation is appropriate?
options: The finding requires at least 5 mm elevation as well as a qualifying ST/S ratio
The finding falls below the excessive-discordance threshold because elevation is under 5 mm
The finding falls below the proportional threshold because ST/S is less than positive 0.25
The discordance meets the proportional modified Sgarbossa criterion and supports urgent occlusion assessment
questions.explanation:
Proportionally Excessive Discordance in LBBB

Correct answer: The discordance meets the proportional modified Sgarbossa criterion and supports urgent occlusion assessment

Use the Sign Convention Correctly

**With an S wave recorded as −8 mm, the ST/S ratio is 3/−8 = −0.375.** This is at or below the −0.25 proportional boundary.

Equivalently, elevation is 37.5% of the S-wave magnitude, exceeding a quarter. The elevation also exceeds the minimum 1 mm used in the modified criterion.

This replaces the older fixed excessive-discordance threshold; it does not mean every expected discordant ST segment is abnormal.

Modified Sgarbossa Criteria

**The modified rule is positive when any one of three components is present:** concordant ST elevation at least 1 mm in a lead with a positive QRS; concordant ST depression at least 1 mm in V1, V2 or V3; or discordant elevation at least 1 mm with signed ST/S ratio at most −0.25.

Check baseline, calibration and lead quality. A negative criterion does not exclude occlusion in a patient with compelling ongoing ischemia.

Use urgent specialist assessment and appropriate reperfusion planning when the integrated picture is concerning. Do not delay necessary care while waiting for a biomarker rise, and do not infer that a positive criterion identifies the exact culprit artery. The original study supports improved detection with proportional assessment, but no ECG rule is perfectly sensitive or specific. Document the measured elevation, S-wave depth and clinical context so the interpretation can be reviewed rather than reduced to LBBB-positive or LBBB-negative.

The finding requires at least 5 mm elevation as well as a qualifying ST/S ratio: The modified proportional criterion requires at least one millimeter of discordant elevation, not a second five-millimeter requirement; three millimeters satisfies the amplitude component.

The finding falls below the excessive-discordance threshold because elevation is under 5 mm: Five millimeters is the original absolute discordance boundary; the modified criterion instead identifies disproportionate elevation relative to S-wave depth, which this lead satisfies.

The finding falls below the proportional threshold because ST/S is less than positive 0.25: The signed ratio uses a negative S-wave amplitude and is compared with minus 0.25 or lower; alternatively compare positive magnitudes, where 37.5 percent exceeds twenty-five percent.

Smith et al. modified Sgarbossa derivation study, 2012 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22939607/

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A patient has persistent crushing chest discomfort. ECG shows upsloping J-point depression across the precordial leads merging into tall symmetric T waves, without conventional anterior ST elevation. Potassium is normal. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Repeat ECGs until conventional anterior elevation appears before activating the pathway
Use serial troponin results to decide whether to activate the emergency invasive pathway
Plan inpatient angiography within twenty-four hours after initial medical stabilization
Arrange emergency coronary occlusion assessment and reperfusion planning
questions.explanation:
de Winter Pattern During Ongoing Ischemic Pain

Correct answer: Arrange emergency coronary occlusion assessment and reperfusion planning

Recognize Occlusion Without Conventional Elevation

**The de Winter pattern combines precordial upsloping depression with prominent symmetric T waves.** It was described in acute LAD occlusion.

Interpret the pattern with the ongoing symptoms, prior tracing and the full ECG. It is not simply a large T wave or an isolated numerical amplitude criterion.

Hyperacute ischemic T waves and evolving occlusion patterns may change over time; obtain serial recordings without delaying escalation.

Do Not Wait for a More Familiar Pattern

**Persistent ischemia with an occlusion-suggestive ECG requires urgent coronary assessment.** Biomarker negativity early after symptom onset does not remove this concern.

Check important mimics such as electrolyte abnormalities in parallel, but do not use a pending test as a reason to postpone necessary care.

The pattern is associated with LAD disease but should not be presented as a perfectly specific map of the culprit in every patient. Definitive anatomy and treatment follow the emergency assessment. Communicate the concern clearly to the receiving team rather than describing the ECG merely as nonspecific ST depression. A working occlusion diagnosis is meant to accelerate an appropriate reperfusion pathway, not to require that every feature of a textbook image be present before action.

Repeat ECGs until conventional anterior elevation appears before activating the pathway: Serial ECGs help identify evolving ischemia and should continue during care, but waiting for conventional elevation can delay reperfusion when the current pattern already suggests occlusion.

Use serial troponin results to decide whether to activate the emergency invasive pathway: Serial biomarkers are appropriate in many stable suspected ACS presentations, but persistent ischemia with this occlusion-suggestive pattern warrants escalation before biochemical confirmation.

Plan inpatient angiography within twenty-four hours after initial medical stabilization: An early inpatient approach suits selected stable high-risk NSTE-ACS, but ongoing pain with an occlusion-suggestive ECG requires more immediate assessment than that planned interval.

questions.question: During ongoing chest discomfort, a patient has horizontal ST depression in multiple inferolateral leads with ST elevation in aVR. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Acute left-main coronary thrombosis established from the ECG
A high-risk global ischemic pattern that requires clinical assessment without uniquely identifying left-main occlusion
Severe three-vessel coronary disease established from the ECG
Secondary ischemia from a systemic supply–demand trigger established from the ECG
questions.explanation:
Diffuse ST Depression With aVR Elevation

Correct answer: A high-risk global ischemic pattern that requires clinical assessment without uniquely identifying left-main occlusion

Describe the Ischemic Pattern Before the Anatomy

**Widespread ST depression with aVR elevation can reflect global subendocardial ischemia.** Left-main or multivessel coronary disease belongs in the differential.

The same appearance can occur during severe supply–demand imbalance and other presentations. The ECG does not independently establish acute left-main thrombosis.

Evaluate symptoms, blood pressure, rhythm, oxygenation and the extent and evolution of changes.

Let Instability and Persistent Ischemia Determine Urgency

**Hemodynamic compromise or refractory symptoms require urgent escalation.** A high-risk pattern should not be placed in a low-risk pathway merely because regional elevation is absent.

Treat a reversible trigger when present while reassessing whether an acute primary coronary process remains plausible. Persistent changes after correction warrant continued concern.

Use the full clinical evidence to plan invasive assessment and antithrombotic treatment, considering important alternative emergencies and bleeding risk. A precise handover distinguishes the observed ECG from an unconfirmed anatomic diagnosis. Avoid the opposite errors of overcalling one specific lesion and underreacting to a potentially extensive ischemic burden. Serial comparison can clarify evolution, but observation should not delay intervention when the patient is unstable.

Acute left-main coronary thrombosis established from the ECG: Left-main disease is an important possibility, but this appearance does not distinguish acute thrombosis from severe multivessel disease or global supply–demand ischemia without further assessment.

Severe three-vessel coronary disease established from the ECG: Multivessel disease can cause this pattern, but angiographic anatomy cannot be determined definitively from the ECG; an acute left-main process and systemic mismatch remain alternatives.

Secondary ischemia from a systemic supply–demand trigger established from the ECG: Severe anemia, hypoxemia or hemodynamic stress can produce global ischemia, but the tracing alone does not establish such a trigger or exclude a primary acute coronary process.

questions.question: A patient has repeated episodes of ischemic discomfort with transient ST elevation that resolves between attacks. Pain and ECG changes recur despite initial treatment. Under the 2023 ESC ACS framework, which approach is appropriate?
options: Immediate invasive assessment for recurrent ischemia with dynamic ECG changes
Arrange early inpatient angiography within twenty-four hours after serial biomarker assessment
Continue medical treatment and reserve angiography for persistent ST elevation
Begin a calcium antagonist trial and defer angiography until the symptom response is assessed
questions.explanation:
Recurrent Transient ST Elevation Is Not a Reassuring Resolution

Correct answer: Immediate invasive assessment for recurrent ischemia with dynamic ECG changes

Distinguish Resolved High-Risk Features From Ongoing Instability

**Recurrent or refractory ischemia and repeated dynamic ECG changes support an immediate invasive strategy.** A normalized tracing between attacks does not erase the clinical sequence.

A stable patient after one resolved transient episode has a different risk context from this patient with recurrence despite treatment.

Document ECGs during symptoms and after resolution rather than using only the latest apparently improved tracing.

Escalate While Continuing Monitored Care

**Continue rhythm and hemodynamic monitoring and urgent cardiology coordination.** Reassess the mechanism and treatment response while arranging definitive evaluation.

Troponin adds information about injury but does not need to become positive before persistent high-risk ischemia is addressed.

The distinction between immediate and early assessment depends on the current clinical state, not simply an isolated score or an ECG label. If a vasomotor mechanism is eventually established, tailor treatment accordingly; do not presume it from nitrate response or transient changes alone. Communicate recurrent episodes clearly at handover so that an asymptomatic interval is not mistaken for a low-risk presentation. The purpose of serial evaluation is to detect this evolving risk and act on it, rather than collect additional normal intervals while ischemia continues.

Arrange early inpatient angiography within twenty-four hours after serial biomarker assessment: An early inpatient strategy suits stable high-risk features, but recurrent ischemia despite treatment with repeated dynamic changes supports immediate assessment without waiting for biomarker confirmation.

Continue medical treatment and reserve angiography for persistent ST elevation: Persistent elevation identifies a familiar emergency pathway, but repeated transient elevation during refractory ischemia is itself a very-high-risk feature; waiting for persistence can delay indicated intervention.

Begin a calcium antagonist trial and defer angiography until the symptom response is assessed: Calcium antagonists are appropriate for established vasospastic angina, but reversibility alone does not establish spasm; a treatment trial should not postpone assessment of this recurrent unstable presentation.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A patient has sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward, a friction rub, widespread ST elevation and PR depression. There is no territorial reciprocal depression apart from expected changes in aVR. Which diagnosis best fits the integrated presentation?
options: A persistent post-infarct ventricular aneurysm pattern
Acute territorial coronary occlusion
Benign early repolarization
Acute pericarditis
questions.explanation:
Pericarditis Versus a Territorial Coronary Pattern

Correct answer: Acute pericarditis

Integrate the Symptoms and Examination With the ECG

**Widespread elevation with PR depression supports pericarditis in the appropriate inflammatory presentation.** The rub and positional pleuritic pain provide independent clinical evidence.

ST shape alone is insufficient: concavity does not reliably exclude coronary occlusion, and inflammatory disease can occasionally produce regional findings.

Under ESC 2025, a definite clinical pericarditis diagnosis requires a compatible presentation with more than one additional criterion; one supports possible pericarditis. This stem supplies both a rub and characteristic ECG changes. These are separate criteria; PR depression and widespread elevation are components of the same ECG category, not two independent categories.

Assess Extent and Complications

**Obtain appropriate echocardiography, inflammatory markers and myocardial-injury assessment.** Effusion, ventricular dysfunction or elevated troponin can change the evaluation.

Consider myocardial involvement and important alternative causes when the presentation is atypical or severe. A pericarditis diagnosis does not imply that coronary disease cannot coexist.

If coronary occlusion remains plausible, resolve it urgently. Assess tamponade, significant effusion, myocardial involvement and secondary causes before disposition. Elevated troponin suggests associated myocardial injury rather than providing an additional pericarditis biomarker criterion. Treatment and follow-up depend on this full assessment, not ST morphology alone.

Additional pericarditis criterion: ESC 2025 | Finding

Examination | Pericardial friction rub

ECG | PR depression or widespread ST elevation

Inflammatory biomarker | Raised CRP

Echocardiography | New or worsening pericardial effusion

CMR | Pericardial edema or late gadolinium enhancement

A persistent post-infarct ventricular aneurysm pattern: An aneurysm can produce persistent regional ST elevation after an infarct, usually with supporting history and Q-wave or imaging evidence; it does not match the acute widespread inflammatory pattern here.

Acute territorial coronary occlusion: Coronary occlusion remains an important alternative in chest pain, but the positional pleuritic symptoms, rub and widespread PR/ST pattern favor pericardial inflammation rather than one coronary territory.

Benign early repolarization: Early repolarization can cause widespread elevation, but does not explain a new friction rub and the stated inflammatory pain pattern as well as acute pericarditis.

ESC myocarditis and pericarditis guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192

Joint ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF Fifth Universal Definition of MI, 2026 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13523810/

questions.topic: STEMI reperfusion and post-lysis management
questions.question: A patient presents to a non-PCI hospital two hours after STEMI symptoms began. Transfer can achieve first device activation 105 minutes after first medical contact. There is no reason that transport is unsafe. Under the 2025 ACC/AHA framework, which reperfusion strategy is preferred?
options: Immediate transfer for primary PCI
Immediate fibrinolysis because the expected interval exceeds ninety minutes
Fibrinolysis followed by primary PCI on arrival regardless of reperfusion response
Antithrombotic stabilization with elective angiography after symptoms settle
questions.explanation:
Timely Primary PCI in a Transfer Patient

Correct answer: Immediate transfer for primary PCI

Use the Correct Clock and Presentation Pathway

**The 2025 ACC/AHA transfer goal is first-medical-contact to device activation within 120 minutes.** The direct-presentation goal is within ninety minutes.

This patient’s anticipated 105-minute transfer pathway fits the stated primary PCI goal. Begin activation and transfer promptly rather than using the goal as permission for avoidable delay.

Keep total symptom duration separate from the system interval; both inform the clinical context.

Coordinate Treatment During Transfer

**Provide monitored ACS care and the appropriate antithrombotic plan while arranging PCI.** Screen for shock, bleeding and important alternative emergencies.

Communicate the ECG, symptom onset and actual expected device time with the receiving team. A nominal transport time is not the same as an achievable reperfusion time.

If the plan becomes delayed, reassess the strategy rather than assuming the original estimate remains true. Primary PCI and a pharmaco-invasive pathway are distinct strategies; giving a lytic simply because the ambulance is leaving for a PCI center is not an equivalent default. The preference is timely effective reperfusion with the least justified treatment burden, guided by the named system and patient eligibility.

Immediate fibrinolysis because the expected interval exceeds ninety minutes: Ninety minutes is the system goal for direct presentation, while the transfer framework allows a goal up to 120 minutes; the stated 105-minute interval supports primary PCI.

Fibrinolysis followed by primary PCI on arrival regardless of reperfusion response: A pharmaco-invasive pathway is appropriate when timely primary PCI is unavailable, but routine lysis before an already timely PCI adds risk without being the preferred strategy here.

Antithrombotic stabilization with elective angiography after symptoms settle: An eligible early STEMI requires urgent reperfusion, not a plan to await spontaneous symptom resolution before elective coronary assessment.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.topic: STEMI reperfusion and post-lysis management
questions.question: A patient presents two hours after clear STEMI onset. Predicted diagnosis-to-wire-crossing time is 190 minutes despite an organized transfer plan. There is no fibrinolytic contraindication and treatment can be given promptly. Under 2023 ESC guidance, which strategy is appropriate?
options: Transfer for primary PCI without fibrinolysis at the predicted 190-minute delay
Prompt fibrinolysis followed by immediate transfer into a pharmaco-invasive pathway
Give fibrinolysis and arrange transfer only if reperfusion fails
Give fibrinolysis and transfer for immediate routine PCI regardless of the reperfusion response
questions.explanation:
Fibrinolysis When Timely Primary PCI Is Unavailable

Correct answer: Prompt fibrinolysis followed by immediate transfer into a pharmaco-invasive pathway

Apply the ESC Reperfusion Threshold

**When PCI-mediated reperfusion cannot be achieved within 120 minutes of STEMI diagnosis, eligible patients within twelve hours of onset should receive fibrinolysis.** This case is well within the symptom window.

ESC targets prompt lytic administration, within ten minutes of diagnosis, when that strategy is selected and the contraindication screen is complete.

The named diagnosis-to-wire clock differs in wording from the ACC/AHA first-medical-contact-to-device framework; report the clock explicitly.

Treat Lysis as the Beginning of an Invasive Pathway

**Transfer immediately to a PCI-capable center after treatment.** Monitor symptoms, ST resolution, rhythm, hemodynamics and bleeding.

Failed reperfusion requires rescue assessment; successful lysis still leads to a planned early invasive strategy rather than discharge from the initial facility.

Select the lytic and concomitant antithrombotics using age, weight, renal function and the current protocol. Fibrinolysis is not an indiscriminate treatment for all troponin-positive ACS or all ST depression. Verify the reperfusion diagnosis and contraindications while avoiding unnecessary delay. The decision reflects the balance between the benefit of earlier reperfusion and the bleeding risk, not a claim that lysis and PCI are interchangeable in every setting.

Transfer for primary PCI without fibrinolysis at the predicted 190-minute delay: Direct primary PCI is preferred when timely or when lysis is unsuitable, but this eligible early presenter exceeds the ESC 120-minute diagnosis-to-reperfusion threshold.

Give fibrinolysis and arrange transfer only if reperfusion fails: Failure requires rescue PCI, but success also requires immediate transfer and planned early angiography; making transfer conditional on failure omits the successful-lysis pathway.

Give fibrinolysis and transfer for immediate routine PCI regardless of the reperfusion response: Immediate rescue PCI is appropriate after failed lysis or instability; after successful uncomplicated lysis, routine angiography is planned at 2–24 hours rather than using an automatic immediate facilitated-PCI strategy.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.topic: STEMI reperfusion and post-lysis management
questions.question: An otherwise eligible early STEMI patient cannot receive timely primary PCI. Which history is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis under the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS framework?
options: Prolonged resuscitation with possible chest-wall trauma
An ischemic stroke five years earlier without residual deficit
Current pregnancy without active bleeding
A spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage six years earlier
questions.explanation:
Prior Intracranial Hemorrhage and STEMI Fibrinolysis

Correct answer: A spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage six years earlier

Distinguish Absolute From Relative Contraindications

**Any prior intracranial hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication in this STEMI framework.** A long interval does not convert it into a low-risk remote ischemic stroke history.

Other critical exclusions include active important bleeding and suspected aortic dissection. Review the complete current checklist rather than asking only about one neurologic event.

Remote ischemic stroke, pregnancy and traumatic resuscitation require individualized assessment of relative risk and alternatives.

Choose a Reperfusion Pathway That Remains Available

**A contraindication to lysis does not remove the need for reperfusion assessment.** Arrange urgent PCI-capable transfer and specialist coordination.

Confirm the stroke type from records when uncertainty can be resolved rapidly; do not assume every past event was ischemic or use an unreliable description to override risk.

Assess blood pressure, medicines, recent surgery, trauma and bleeding in parallel. The table summarizes the 2025 ACC/AHA STEMI framework, whose time windows differ from some other guidance. Its acute ischemic stroke exception concerns a separate indication and specialist eligibility assessment; it is not blanket permission to give the STEMI lytic regimen in concurrent stroke. Document the contraindication and alternative reperfusion plan clearly.

Clinical feature | Absolute exclusion in ACC/AHA 2025 | Relative concern in the same framework

Intracranial disease | Any prior ICH; cerebral vascular lesion; malignant intracranial neoplasm | Other known intracranial pathology; dementia

Prior ischemic stroke | Within 3 months, with the guideline’s acute-stroke exception | More than 3 months earlier

Head injury or neurosurgery | Significant closed-head/facial trauma within 3 months; intracranial/intraspinal surgery within 2 months | Assess other trauma according to site and severity

Blood pressure | SBP >180 or DBP >110 mmHg unresponsive to treatment | Same elevation at presentation before treatment; chronic severe poor control

Bleeding or aortic disease | Active bleeding/bleeding diathesis excluding menses; suspected dissection | Internal bleeding within 2–4 weeks; active peptic ulcer; oral anticoagulant treatment

Recent procedures | Intracranial/intraspinal surgery as above | Major surgery within 3 weeks; noncompressible vascular puncture

Other relative concerns | Assess all absolute exclusions first | Traumatic/prolonged CPR >10 minutes; pregnancy

Prolonged resuscitation with possible chest-wall trauma: Traumatic or prolonged CPR increases bleeding concern and requires assessment, but is a relative consideration rather than the particular absolute history asked for here.

An ischemic stroke five years earlier without residual deficit: A remote ischemic stroke requires careful assessment and is a relative contraindication in the stated framework; it is not equivalent to any previous intracranial hemorrhage.

Current pregnancy without active bleeding: Pregnancy is an important relative bleeding-risk consideration, but is not classified as the same absolute prohibition as the supplied prior intracranial hemorrhage.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A 62-year-old weighing 84 kg is selected for fibrinolysis for STEMI. Using the standard adult STEMI weight-tier regimen without an older-patient dose reduction, what is the tenecteplase dose?
options: 40 mg as a single IV bolus
45 mg as a single IV bolus
50 mg as a single IV bolus
25 mg as a single IV bolus
questions.explanation:
Weight-Based Tenecteplase for STEMI

Correct answer: 45 mg as a single IV bolus

Use the Indication-Specific Weight Table

**The standard STEMI tenecteplase regimen uses weight tiers rather than one fixed dose for all adults.** At 84 kg, the applicable tier is ==45 mg==.

Check the vial, reconstituted concentration and delivery instructions. A dose stated in milligrams should not be converted to milliliters without confirming the preparation.

Do not substitute an acute ischemic stroke regimen merely because the drug name is the same.

Complete the Fibrinolysis Prescription

**The lytic is only one component of treatment.** Appropriate antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, monitoring and immediate transfer are also required.

The ESC 2023 fibrinolysis recommendation advises considering half-dose tenecteplase in patients older than seventy-five years. Thus an otherwise eligible older patient in the 80-to-below-90-kg tier would receive 22.5 mg under that modified regimen, rather than the standard 45 mg. The sixty-two-year-old in this stem is outside that age modification. Keep the guideline age wording and local protocol explicit rather than confusing this reduction with a stroke dose.

Review contraindications, weight reliability, recent antithrombotic exposure and bleeding risk before administration. Observe for neurologic symptoms and other bleeding after treatment. A correct numerical dose does not establish that the patient was eligible for fibrinolysis or that reperfusion succeeded. Assess the subsequent ECG and clinical response and use the rescue or planned angiographic pathway as appropriate. Keep indication and protocol visible in the prescription to prevent confusion between different tenecteplase uses.

Body weight | Standard STEMI dose

<60 kg | 30 mg

60 to <70 kg | 35 mg

70 to <80 kg | 40 mg

80 to <90 kg | 45 mg

≥90 kg | 50 mg

40 mg as a single IV bolus: Forty milligrams is the standard STEMI tier for weight at least 70 but below 80 kg; this patient weighs 84 kg.

50 mg as a single IV bolus: Fifty milligrams is the standard maximum tier for weight at least 90 kg, rather than the 80-to-below-90-kg tier supplied here.

25 mg as a single IV bolus: Twenty-five milligrams is not the standard full-dose STEMI tier for this patient; it can arise in a different indication or an explicitly modified regimen.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

questions.question: A 68-year-old is receiving STEMI fibrinolysis and aspirin. There is no P2Y12 contraindication. Which oral P2Y12 regimen matches the 2025 ACC/AHA recommendation at fibrinolytic administration?
options: Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily
Clopidogrel 75 mg daily without a loading dose
Clopidogrel 300 mg loading, then 75 mg daily
Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Clopidogrel at the Time of STEMI Fibrinolysis

Correct answer: Clopidogrel 300 mg loading, then 75 mg daily

Use the Reperfusion-Specific Regimen

**Clopidogrel is the recommended oral P2Y12 adjunct at fibrinolysis in the stated framework.** At age below seventy-five, use ==300 mg loading followed by 75 mg daily==.

The 2025 ACC/AHA narrative uses age at least seventy-five for the no-load 75 mg regimen, whereas its Table 7 uses older than seventy-five; ESC 2023 also uses older than seventy-five. Thus the exact seventy-fifth-year boundary is not internally consistent across these presentations. Follow the applicable local protocol at that boundary; this sixty-eight-year-old case is unambiguous and does not test the discrepancy.

Do not transfer a primary-PCI preference for another P2Y12 agent directly into the initial lysis prescription.

Complete and Reconcile Concomitant Treatment

**Aspirin and a suitable parenteral anticoagulant are also part of the pathway.** Select and dose the anticoagulant using age, weight and renal function.

For example, the cited enoxaparin lysis regimen below age seventy-five with adequate renal function begins with 30 mg IV, then 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every twelve hours, with the first two doses capped at 100 mg.

That example must not be copied to older patients or severe renal impairment without adjustment. Record all pretransfer doses and times so the receiving PCI team avoids duplication. Monitor for bleeding and assess reperfusion while arranging transfer. Later switching or procedural loading decisions depend on elapsed time, previous exposure and the invasive plan; the initial clopidogrel choice does not supply permission for an unplanned extra load of another agent.

Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily: Ticagrelor has an important role in ACS, particularly PCI pathways, but is not the recommended initial oral P2Y12 regimen given concurrently with fibrinolysis here.

Clopidogrel 75 mg daily without a loading dose: A no-loading regimen is used in older fibrinolysis patients; the sixty-eight-year-old in this question is clearly within the loading-dose group.

Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily: Prasugrel is used in selected PCI-treated ACS patients after appropriate assessment, rather than as the standard P2Y12 adjunct at fibrinolytic administration.

questions.topic: STEMI reperfusion and post-lysis management
questions.question: Ninety minutes after fibrinolysis, a patient still has ischemic chest pain and only 20% resolution of the initial ST elevation. Which next strategy is appropriate?
options: Continue medical treatment and repeat the ECG at three hours before deciding on rescue
Give a second fibrinolytic dose and reassess after another ninety minutes
Wait for routine angiography in the two-to-twenty-four-hour window
Immediate angiography with rescue PCI when indicated
questions.explanation:
Failed Fibrinolysis Requires Rescue Assessment

Correct answer: Immediate angiography with rescue PCI when indicated

Assess Reperfusion at the Appropriate Time

**ST resolution below 50% at sixty to ninety minutes supports failed fibrinolysis.** Persistent pain strengthens the concern in this case.

Hemodynamic or electrical instability, worsening ischemia or evidence of reocclusion can also require immediate angiography rather than waiting for a scheduled reassessment.

A transient rhythm change or partial symptom improvement does not override ongoing concerning evidence.

Separate Rescue PCI From Planned Early Angiography

**Rescue PCI addresses failure or renewed occlusion.** Successful fibrinolysis still requires transfer and early angiography, but it is a different clinical pathway.

Communicate the lytic agent, timing, antiplatelets, anticoagulants and subsequent ECG response to the receiving team.

Continue monitoring and evaluate bleeding while urgent transport and catheterization are coordinated. Repeat fibrinolysis is discouraged in this setting rather than treated as an interchangeable second attempt. Do not await enzyme completion, a further routine ward review or proof of an unfavorable outcome before acting. The decision follows the current reperfusion evidence and patient stability, with angiography determining the anatomy and appropriate intervention.

Continue medical treatment and repeat the ECG at three hours before deciding on rescue: Later reassessment can be useful when initial findings are equivocal, but persistent ischemic pain with only twenty-percent ST resolution at ninety minutes already supports failed reperfusion and should prompt immediate rescue assessment.

Give a second fibrinolytic dose and reassess after another ninety minutes: Repeat lysis is not the recommended rescue strategy for failed reperfusion; urgent angiography addresses persistent occlusion and avoids delaying effective treatment.

Wait for routine angiography in the two-to-twenty-four-hour window: That planned early window applies after successful lysis in a stable patient, whereas persistent pain and poor ST resolution indicate failure requiring immediate assessment.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: After fibrinolysis, a stable patient has resolution of pain and 70% ST-segment resolution at ninety minutes. Under the 2023 ESC pharmaco-invasive pathway, which plan is appropriate?
options: Transfer and routine angiography within two to twenty-four hours of the lytic bolus
Transfer and schedule angiography forty-eight to seventy-two hours after the bolus
Transfer and use recurrent ischemia to determine whether angiography is needed
Transfer for immediate rescue angiography on the basis of residual ST elevation
questions.explanation:
Angiography After Apparently Successful Fibrinolysis

Correct answer: Transfer and routine angiography within two to twenty-four hours of the lytic bolus

Recognize Success Without Ending the Pathway

**Pain relief and substantial ST resolution support successful reperfusion**, but do not prove a normal culprit artery or eliminate recurrence risk.

In the ESC framework, routine angiography follows within ==2–24 hours from the lytic bolus==, with PCI if required.

Transfer to the PCI-capable center begins promptly; it is not postponed until the intended catheterization time.

Escalate if the Clinical State Changes

**Recurrent ischemia, failed reperfusion or instability moves the patient into an immediate rescue pathway.** Do not retain a routine schedule when the indication changes.

Continue ECG, rhythm, hemodynamic and bleeding surveillance. Reconcile all antiplatelet and anticoagulant doses before the procedure.

The planned early strategy differs from routine facilitated immediate PCI after giving lysis to a patient who could already receive timely primary PCI. Describe the indication and timing clearly to avoid confusing those pathways. A reperfusion arrhythmia is supportive information, not a reason to stop monitoring or omit angiography. The clinical sequence remains lytic selection, transfer, response assessment and the appropriate invasive step, with treatment adjusted to the patient’s evolving condition.

Transfer and schedule angiography forty-eight to seventy-two hours after the bolus: A later inpatient schedule can be considered in other clinical settings, but it misses the recommended two-to-twenty-four-hour routine invasive window after successful fibrinolysis.

Transfer and use recurrent ischemia to determine whether angiography is needed: An ischemia-guided selective strategy is used in selected other presentations, but successful lysis still requires routine early angiographic assessment under this pharmaco-invasive framework.

Transfer for immediate rescue angiography on the basis of residual ST elevation: Immediate rescue is appropriate for failed lysis, recurrent ischemia or instability; seventy-percent resolution with relief of pain and stability does not meet that stated failure pattern.

questions.question: Four days after a completed infarct, a patient is stable and asymptomatic without ongoing ischemia, severe acute heart failure or life-threatening arrhythmia. Angiography shows a persistently occluded infarct-related artery. Which principle is appropriate?
options: Perform elective infarct-artery PCI if any residual viability is detected
Perform routine infarct-artery PCI during the current admission
Schedule infarct-artery PCI after four weeks of medical stabilization
Do not perform routine PCI solely to reopen the completed-infarct artery in this stable setting
questions.explanation:
Late Presentation With a Stable Completed Infarct

Correct answer: Do not perform routine PCI solely to reopen the completed-infarct artery in this stable setting

Distinguish a Completed Infarct From Ongoing Salvageable Ischemia

**Routine PCI beyond forty-eight hours is not supported solely to open an occluded infarct artery in an asymptomatic stable patient.** This is a clinical-population qualification, not a prohibition on every late intervention.

Ongoing angina, shock, severe acute heart failure or dangerous arrhythmias require a different urgent assessment even when symptom onset was delayed.

Avoid treating the calendar alone as the decision rule; the current clinical state determines whether an active indication remains.

Continue Comprehensive Post-Infarct Care

**Assess ventricular function, complications and secondary prevention needs.** Lack of a routine late-opening indication does not mean that treatment or follow-up is complete.

OAT tested routine PCI versus medical therapy in selected stable patients with persistent infarct-artery occlusion three to twenty-eight days after MI. Routine opening did not reduce its composite of death, reinfarction or NYHA class IV heart failure.

Other coronary lesions, recurrent symptoms or a separate revascularization indication require their own assessment. Residual viability was present in many patients assessed in an OAT ancillary study, so this evidence is not simply a comparison restricted to completely nonviable infarcts. Medical therapy, rehabilitation and risk-factor care remain essential. Document whether ongoing ischemia exists. If the condition changes, reassess rather than retaining a conclusion derived from an earlier stable presentation.

Perform elective infarct-artery PCI if any residual viability is detected: Viability can inform selected complex assessments, but residual viable tissue alone is not an automatic indication for routine late opening; symptoms, ischemic burden, anatomy and clinical context remain relevant.

Perform routine infarct-artery PCI during the current admission: Routine late opening has not improved the expected clinical outcomes in the stable completed-infarct population; ongoing ischemia or another independent indication would change the assessment.

Schedule infarct-artery PCI after four weeks of medical stabilization: Staged PCI is useful for selected residual significant disease, but delaying this procedure does not create an indication to open a stable completed-infarct artery solely for patency.

questions.topic: NSTE-ACS risk and invasive strategy
questions.question: A patient with NSTE-ACS develops sustained ventricular tachycardia requiring cardioversion, with continued ischemic discomfort afterward. There is no persistent diagnostic ST elevation. Which invasive strategy is appropriate?
options: Immediate angiography with intent to revascularize if indicated
Early angiography within twenty-four hours after routine ward stabilization
A selective strategy after predischarge stress imaging
An inpatient angiogram after forty-eight to seventy-two hours of rhythm observation
questions.explanation:
Electrical Instability in NSTE-ACS

Correct answer: Immediate angiography with intent to revascularize if indicated

Recognize Very-High-Risk Features Without Requiring STEMI

**Electrical instability with ongoing ischemia supports an immediate invasive strategy.** A conventional ST-elevation pattern is not required for every coronary emergency.

Resuscitate the arrhythmia and correct reversible contributors while the coronary pathway is activated. Treatment and investigation proceed together.

Hemodynamic instability or refractory ischemia are other reasons not to wait for a routine early slot.

Use the Patient’s Current State to Set Urgency

**Risk scores and biomarker timing do not override active instability.** The clinical event supplies an actionable risk feature.

Continue monitoring, defibrillation capability and appropriate ACS treatment during transfer or catheterization preparation.

Angiography identifies the coronary anatomy; revascularization depends on the findings and feasibility. Do not assume every ventricular arrhythmia has a coronary cause, but do not dismiss the demonstrated ischemic context because the ECG lacks persistent elevation. Document the rhythm, treatment and post-cardioversion symptoms so the receiving team understands why this is an immediate rather than simply an early investigation. A subsequently normal rhythm does not erase the significance of the event that prompted escalation.

Early angiography within twenty-four hours after routine ward stabilization: A within-day strategy is appropriate for selected stable high-risk patients, but the life-threatening electrical instability and continuing ischemia warrant immediate assessment.

A selective strategy after predischarge stress imaging: Stress-based selection is inappropriate during ongoing ischemia with sustained VT; the patient has an urgent invasive indication.

An inpatient angiogram after forty-eight to seventy-two hours of rhythm observation: A delayed inpatient approach may be selected in stable patients with different risk profiles, but sustained VT with continuing ischemia requires immediate invasive assessment rather than observation for recurrence.

Correct answer: A — Immediate angiography with intent to revascularize if indicated

  • Electrical instability with ongoing ischemia supports an immediate invasive strategy. A conventional ST-elevation pattern is not required for every coronary emergency.
    • Resuscitate the arrhythmia and correct reversible contributors while the coronary pathway is activated. Treatment and investigation proceed together.
    • Hemodynamic instability or refractory ischemia are other reasons not to wait for a routine early slot.

  • Risk scores and biomarker timing do not override active instability. The clinical event supplies an actionable risk feature.
    • Continue monitoring, defibrillation capability and appropriate ACS treatment during transfer or catheterization preparation.

Document the rhythm, treatment and post-cardioversion symptoms so the receiving team understands why this is an immediate rather than simply an early investigation. A subsequently normal rhythm does not erase the significance of the event that prompted escalation.

questions.explanation:
Stable High-Risk NSTE-ACS and Early Angiography

Correct answer: An inpatient invasive strategy with angiography within twenty-four hours considered

Separate the Invasive Plan From Its Exact Timing

**An inpatient invasive strategy is appropriate in confirmed NSTEMI.** In the 2023 ESC framework, high-risk findings such as GRACE above 140 support considering angiography within twenty-four hours.

This is distinct from an immediate strategy for very-high-risk clinical instability. The stem explicitly describes a stabilized patient.

The wording and recommendation strength should be attributed to the named guideline rather than presented as an identical rule across every source and year.

Reassess While Awaiting the Procedure

**New refractory pain, shock, acute ischemic heart failure or dangerous arrhythmia changes the urgency.** A planned early slot is not a reason to wait through deterioration.

Review bleeding risk, renal function, comorbidity and the antithrombotic plan alongside ischemic risk.

Trials of early versus delayed angiography vary in eligibility and actual timing; do not infer identical mortality benefit for all risk groups. The ESC 2023 table distinguishes an inpatient invasive strategy from the recommendation to consider an early procedure. Continue monitored reassessment because new very-high-risk findings supersede the planned timetable.

ESC 2023 group | Qualifying findings | Invasive approach

Very high risk | Hemodynamic instability/shock; refractory or recurrent pain despite treatment; life-threatening arrhythmia; mechanical complication; ACS-related HF; recurrent dynamic ST/T changes, especially intermittent elevation | Immediate invasive strategy

High risk | Confirmed NSTEMI; GRACE >140; dynamic ST/T changes; transient ST elevation | Inpatient invasive strategy; angiography within 24 hours should be considered

No very-high/high-risk criteria | Assess residual clinical suspicion, comorbidity and test findings | Individualize inpatient assessment or selective invasive evaluation

Emergency angiography solely because GRACE exceeds 140: A score above 140 supports high risk and consideration of early angiography, but does not by itself create the same immediate indication as shock, refractory ischemia or electrical instability.

Outpatient angiography after noninvasive stress testing: Confirmed NSTEMI with this risk profile supports an inpatient invasive approach rather than routine outpatient stress-based triage.

A selective invasive strategy based on a negative predischarge stress test: Selective testing may guide care in appropriately assessed lower-risk presentations, but established NSTEMI with GRACE 156 supports an inpatient invasive strategy even while symptoms are controlled.

options: Obtain the next scheduled troponin to confirm recurrent injury before escalating

questions.explanation:
An Admission Risk Score Does Not Override New Instability

Correct answer: The new clinical instability requires immediate reassessment and invasive escalation despite the earlier score

Use Risk Prediction for Its Intended Purpose

**GRACE estimates clinical risk from defined patient variables.** It helps stratify patients but is not a guarantee of a stable future course.

Age, hemodynamics, renal function, heart failure severity, arrest, ECG and biomarker information contribute in the relevant score version.

Use a validated calculator and the correct version rather than reconstructing a score from an incomplete list or mixing models for different outcomes.

Reassess the Evolving Patient

**New refractory ischemia and hypotension change the clinical pathway.** Stabilize, investigate complications and coordinate urgent invasive assessment.

Do not wait for another laboratory value or an updated score to cross a threshold when the urgent indication is already present.

Document the change from the admission state and communicate it clearly to the receiving team. Risk scores summarize selected evidence; they do not encode every dangerous complication or remove the need for serial examination. Conversely, a high predicted risk in a stable patient is not the same as the immediate clinical emergency described here. Keep the reason for urgency tied to the actual deterioration so later clinicians do not mistake it for an elective timing preference.

Obtain the next scheduled troponin to confirm recurrent injury before escalating: Serial troponin helps characterize injury, but hemodynamic deterioration and refractory pain require urgent action even before another biomarker change is demonstrated.

Recalculate GRACE and use the updated category to select the angiography time: Recalculation may document changing risk, but current refractory ischemia and hypotension already justify immediate escalation; the updated score is not a prerequisite.

Intensify anti-ischemic therapy and retain the early inpatient angiography slot: Medical stabilization proceeds alongside urgent assessment; retaining a nonemergency slot underweights the new instability and may delay treatment of ongoing coronary compromise.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191
