questions.question: A stable NSTE-ACS patient has unknown coronary anatomy and angiography planned in four hours. Under the 2023 ESC approach, which P2Y12 strategy is appropriate?
options: Defer routine oral P2Y12 loading until anatomy and the revascularization plan are known
Give prasugrel 60 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory
Give ticagrelor 180 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory
Give clopidogrel 600 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory
questions.explanation:
P2Y12 Pretreatment Before Early Angiography

Correct answer: Defer routine oral P2Y12 loading until anatomy and the revascularization plan are known

Define Pretreatment Precisely

**Pretreatment means giving a P2Y12 inhibitor before coronary anatomy is known.** It is a timing decision, not a decision to omit appropriate eventual antiplatelet treatment.

For planned early angiography within twenty-four hours in NSTE-ACS, the 2023 ESC guideline discourages routine pretreatment.

Aspirin and appropriate anticoagulation are separate treatment decisions and are not automatically deferred with the oral P2Y12 load.

Account for Delay and the Possible Treatment Path

**Anatomy may identify a surgical indication or another diagnosis**, so unnecessary early platelet inhibition can add harm without benefit.

If angiography will be substantially delayed, a different individualized pretreatment decision may be appropriate after assessing bleeding risk; the 2025 ACC/AHA guidance permits consideration of upstream clopidogrel or ticagrelor when the delay exceeds twenty-four hours.

Do not transfer the rule unchanged to STEMI or concurrent fibrinolysis. After anatomy is known, select the agent and timing according to PCI, surgery or medical management, comorbidity and contraindications. Record any doses already given during transfer so a deferred strategy does not become accidental duplicate loading when the patient reaches the catheterization laboratory.

Give prasugrel 60 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory: Prasugrel is effective for eligible PCI patients after the treatment decision, but pretreatment before anatomy is known failed to improve ischemic outcomes and increased bleeding in ACCOAST.

Give ticagrelor 180 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory: Ticagrelor is appropriate in eligible ACS treatment and may be considered upstream with substantially delayed angiography, but routine pretreatment is discouraged in this early-invasive unknown-anatomy setting.

Give clopidogrel 600 mg now, before transfer to the catheterization laboratory: Clopidogrel can be selected when potent agents are unsuitable or in other defined pathways, but its lower potency does not remove bleeding or surgical concerns that favor deferral here.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: A surgically suitable patient with diabetes has stabilized after NSTEMI. Angiography shows complex three-vessel disease involving the LAD, with graftable distal vessels. No ongoing instability requires immediate culprit PCI. Which revascularization plan is best supported?
options: Culprit PCI now followed by staged nonculprit PCI after discharge
Complete multivessel PCI during the index hospitalization
Culprit PCI followed by medical treatment of all remaining lesions as the definitive plan
Heart Team assessment favoring CABG after appropriate preparation
questions.explanation:
Choosing CABG After Stabilized NSTE-ACS

Correct answer: Heart Team assessment favoring CABG after appropriate preparation

Select the Method Using Anatomy and Patient Factors

**CABG may be preferred in NSTE-ACS with complex multivessel disease and diabetes involving the LAD.** An acute presentation does not make multivessel PCI the automatic best definitive strategy.

Assess left-main involvement, lesion complexity, ventricular function, distal targets, frailty, renal disease, surgical risk and patient preferences.

A Heart Team discussion is particularly useful when the optimal method is uncertain. A recommendation for surgery assumes feasible grafting and acceptable operative risk.

Prepare Without Losing Control of Ischemic Risk

**Timing balances the current ischemic state with operative bleeding risk.** Review aspirin, oral P2Y12 exposure and anticoagulation with the surgical team.

For elective CABG, the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS table specifies clopidogrel interruption for five days, prasugrel for seven days, and ticagrelor for three to five days. Urgent surgery has a different risk balance; seek at least twenty-four hours of interruption when feasible rather than applying elective intervals as an absolute barrier to life-saving surgery.

Continue evidence-based ACS and secondary prevention treatment while planning revascularization. Explain expected benefits, procedural risks and the possibility of later intervention. PCI remains an important alternative when CABG is unsuitable or the anatomy supports a percutaneous approach. The answer is therefore a patient-specific surgical preference, not a claim that every diabetic patient with any coronary stenosis requires bypass surgery. Document the anatomical and clinical reasons for the selected strategy.

Culprit PCI now followed by staged nonculprit PCI after discharge: Staged PCI is an effective strategy in suitable multivessel anatomy, but it does not address why this patient’s diabetes and complex graftable disease favor selecting CABG before committing to a complete PCI pathway.

Complete multivessel PCI during the index hospitalization: Multivessel PCI is appropriate in selected ACS anatomy or when surgery is unsuitable, but complex three-vessel LAD disease with diabetes favors CABG in this suitable surgical candidate.

Culprit PCI followed by medical treatment of all remaining lesions as the definitive plan: Culprit-only initial PCI is particularly important in shock; this stable patient still needs an anatomy-based plan addressing prognostically important multivessel disease.

questions.question: After successful culprit PCI for STEMI, a patient remains stable without shock. There are severe, PCI-suitable nonculprit stenoses. Using the 2023 ESC framework, which plan best addresses the remaining coronary disease?
options: Restrict treatment permanently to the culprit lesion unless angina recurs
Plan complete revascularization during the index procedure or within forty-five days
Use same-session nonculprit PCI rather than allowing a staged completion plan
Delay any nonculprit intervention for at least three months to establish chronic stability
questions.explanation:
Complete Revascularization After Stable STEMI

Correct answer: Plan complete revascularization during the index procedure or within forty-five days

Apply the Stable-STEMI Evidence to the Correct Population

**Complete revascularization is recommended for suitable significant multivessel disease after STEMI without cardiogenic shock.** The 2023 ESC window is the index procedure or ==within forty-five days==.

Select lesions using angiographic severity and clinical context. This does not mean stenting every visible irregularity or ignoring anatomy that favors surgery.

Timing should account for renal function, contrast already used, procedural complexity and the patient’s condition. A staged strategy is an active treatment plan, not an unstructured deferral.

Understand What COMPLETE Demonstrated

**COMPLETE compared planned nonculprit PCI with culprit-only management after successful culprit PCI.** At a median three years, cardiovascular death or new MI occurred in 7.8% versus 10.5%, respectively.

The trial supports treating important residual disease in the studied stable population. It does not establish that every lesion must be treated immediately or that the same strategy should be used during shock. Continue antithrombotic treatment, lipid lowering and rehabilitation regardless of procedural completeness. Document which lesions remain, their significance and the planned timing so the intended staged procedure is not lost after discharge.

Delay any nonculprit intervention for at least three months to establish chronic stability: A long mandatory delay is not the guideline strategy; suitable complete revascularization is planned during the index procedure or within forty-five days.

questions.question: A patient with acute MI and cardiogenic shock has a clearly identified occluded culprit artery and severe nonculprit stenoses. Culprit PCI is feasible. What is the preferred initial PCI strategy?
options: Treat the culprit vessel now and reassess nonculprit revascularization after stabilization
Perform routine immediate PCI of the culprit and all severe nonculprit lesions
Treat the largest nonculprit territory before the identified culprit vessel
Defer coronary PCI until vasopressors have fully corrected the shock
questions.explanation:
Initial PCI in Infarction With Cardiogenic Shock

Correct answer: Treat the culprit vessel now and reassess nonculprit revascularization after stabilization

Revascularize the Culprit Without Routine Additional PCI

**Cardiogenic shock changes the initial multivessel strategy.** Emergency culprit revascularization is indicated, while routine nonculprit PCI during the same procedure is discouraged.

This differs from the stable-STEMI recommendation for complete revascularization. Do not extrapolate a stable-population benefit into an unstable physiological setting.

Provide shock support, assess ventricular function and look for mechanical complications concurrently. Anatomy unsuitable for PCI may require emergency surgical consideration.

Interpret CULPRIT-SHOCK and Plan Subsequent Care

**CULPRIT-SHOCK allowed staged revascularization after initial culprit-only PCI.** It therefore tested the initial strategy, not permanent abandonment of other important lesions.

At thirty days, death or renal-replacement therapy occurred in 45.9% with culprit-only PCI versus 55.4% with immediate multivessel PCI; relative risk 0.83.

The endpoint was a composite, and the result does not mean that nonculprit disease is harmless or that every shock presentation has an easily identifiable culprit. After stabilization, reassess residual anatomy, symptoms, ventricular recovery, renal function and suitability for PCI or CABG. Avoid adding contrast and procedural complexity merely to achieve an angiographically complete result during the emergency. The initial priority is effective culprit treatment with coordinated support and a documented plan for reassessment.

Perform routine immediate PCI of the culprit and all severe nonculprit lesions: Complete PCI is beneficial in appropriate stable patients, but routine immediate multivessel PCI during shock increases harm compared with the culprit-only initial strategy.

Treat the largest nonculprit territory before the identified culprit vessel: A large residual ischemic territory may matter later, but it does not supersede emergency reperfusion of the clearly identified infarct-related artery in this presentation.

Defer coronary PCI until vasopressors have fully corrected the shock: Hemodynamic support is provided alongside emergency culprit revascularization; waiting for complete resolution leaves the ischemic cause untreated.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

CULPRIT-SHOCK randomized trial, 2017 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1710261

questions.question: Angiography confirms mid-distal LAD spontaneous coronary artery dissection in a patient whose pain has resolved. Distal flow is preserved, there is no left-main involvement, and hemodynamics and serial ECGs are stable. Which initial strategy is most appropriate?
options: Immediate long-segment stenting to seal the entire dissection
Monitored conservative management with reassessment for recurrent ischemia
Immediate CABG for the dissected LAD
Repeat angiography with intravascular imaging before selecting conservative treatment
questions.explanation:
Conservative Management of Stable SCAD

Correct answer: Monitored conservative management with reassessment for recurrent ischemia

Allow Healing When Perfusion and Clinical Stability Permit

**Conservative management is generally preferred in stable SCAD with preserved distal flow and no ongoing ischemia.** Intramural hematoma and arterial-wall disruption differ from a straightforward plaque stenosis.

Many lesions heal spontaneously. Hospital observation and serial assessment remain important because early extension or recurrent ischemia can occur.

PCI can enter the false lumen, propagate hematoma or require extensive stenting. These procedural hazards explain why angiographic narrowing alone does not establish benefit from intervention.

Identify the Exceptions and Individualize Medical Treatment

**Ongoing ischemia, impaired flow, hemodynamic instability or high-risk proximal anatomy prompts urgent specialist reassessment.** The procedure chosen depends on the anatomy and feasibility.

The 2023 ESC recommendation limits PCI to SCAD with ongoing ischemic features, substantial myocardium at risk and reduced antegrade flow. Selected left-main or proximal multivessel disease may require CABG.

Review antithrombotic treatment after the mechanism is established. The AHA statement advises considering discontinuation of systemic anticoagulation without another indication; antiplatelet strategy in conservatively managed SCAD has limited evidence and should not be presented as a universally proven regimen. Stented patients require appropriate stent-directed antiplatelet care. Assess ventricular function, provide individualized rehabilitation and arrange evaluation for associated arteriopathy, including fibromuscular dysplasia. Persistent or recurrent symptoms require clinical assessment rather than automatic attribution to either reinfarction or benign recovery.

Immediate long-segment stenting to seal the entire dissection: PCI may be needed for ongoing ischemia with threatened myocardium and impaired flow, but routine long-segment stenting adds technical risk in a stable, well-perfused dissection.

Immediate CABG for the dissected LAD: CABG is considered for selected high-risk anatomy or failed or unsuitable PCI with ongoing ischemia; LAD involvement alone does not justify surgery in this stable distal lesion.

Repeat angiography with intravascular imaging before selecting conservative treatment: Intravascular imaging can clarify uncertain diagnoses when it changes management, but unnecessary instrumentation of an already established stable SCAD can propagate injury.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

AHA scientific statement on spontaneous coronary artery dissection, 2018 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5957087/

questions.topic: Antiplatelet anticoagulant and bleeding decisions
questions.question: A patient with confirmed ACS can swallow and has no aspirin hypersensitivity or active bleeding. No loading dose has been given. Under the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline, which oral regimen is appropriate?
options: Aspirin 162–325 mg initially, followed by 325 mg daily as the preferred maintenance dose
Aspirin 75–100 mg initially, followed by 75–100 mg daily
Aspirin 162–325 mg initially, followed by 75–100 mg daily
Aspirin 75–100 mg initially, followed by 325 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Aspirin Loading and Maintenance in ACS

Correct answer: Aspirin 162–325 mg initially, followed by 75–100 mg daily

Separate Rapid Platelet Inhibition From Maintenance

**Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase-1 and thromboxane production.** The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS regimen is an oral load of ==162–325 mg== followed by ==75–100 mg daily==.

Use a nonenteric-coated preparation for prompt absorption; chewing the initial dose accelerates its effect when oral administration is suitable.

A history of low-dose aspirin use does not automatically remove the guideline loading recommendation. Confirm what was actually administered during transfer to prevent undocumented duplicate doses.

Integrate Aspirin With the Rest of ACS Treatment

**Aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor act at different platelet pathways.** The accompanying agent and treatment duration depend on reperfusion strategy, bleeding risk and other indications for anticoagulation.

Active pathological bleeding or a serious hypersensitivity history requires an alternative specialist plan. Gastrointestinal risk should prompt assessment and appropriate gastroprotection rather than indiscriminate high-dose maintenance.

Low-dose maintenance provides effective thromboxane suppression. Trials have not established superior clinical protection from maintaining the acute loading range, and some ACS comparisons showed more gastrointestinal or minor bleeding with higher doses. Reassess the regimen when bleeding occurs or oral anticoagulation is needed; the initial recommendation does not imply that aspirin must continue unchanged through every later combination strategy. Give clear discharge instructions distinguishing the loading dose already received from the ongoing daily dose.

Aspirin 162–325 mg initially, followed by 325 mg daily as the preferred maintenance dose: The initial loading range is appropriate, but prolonged full-dose aspirin is not the preferred maintenance strategy and adds bleeding burden without established superior ACS protection.

Aspirin 75–100 mg initially, followed by 75–100 mg daily: Low-dose aspirin is suitable maintenance treatment, but a larger initial loading dose is recommended to establish prompt platelet inhibition during ACS.

Aspirin 75–100 mg initially, followed by 325 mg daily: This reverses the intended loading and maintenance approach: the acute phase requires a loading dose, while subsequent treatment generally uses low-dose aspirin.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: A 62-year-old patient weighing 76 kg undergoes PCI for NSTEMI. There was an ischemic stroke five years earlier, without intracranial hemorrhage. Bleeding risk is not high, oral anticoagulation is unnecessary, and ticagrelor is tolerated and affordable. Which oral P2Y12 regimen is preferred among these choices?
options: Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily
Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily
Clopidogrel 600 mg loading, then 75 mg daily
Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 60 mg twice daily
questions.explanation:
P2Y12 Selection After a Previous Ischemic Stroke

Correct answer: Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 90 mg twice daily

Distinguish Ischemic Stroke From Intracranial Hemorrhage

**Previous stroke or TIA excludes prasugrel**, irrespective of the reassuring age and weight in this vignette. Reducing the prasugrel dose does not remove that restriction.

A remote ischemic stroke is not the same contraindication as previous intracranial hemorrhage for ticagrelor. Review the actual diagnosis rather than accepting an unspecified history of stroke.

For an eligible ACS patient undergoing PCI, the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline favors ticagrelor or prasugrel over clopidogrel; the prior stroke directs selection away from prasugrel.

Prescribe and Monitor the Selected Agent

**The initial ACS ticagrelor regimen is a 180 mg load followed by 90 mg twice daily.** Check prior loading during transfer before prescribing another dose.

Monitor bleeding, dyspnea and clinically important bradyarrhythmia. Review strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers and adherence to twice-daily treatment.

Active pathological bleeding or previous intracranial hemorrhage precludes ticagrelor. Clopidogrel remains useful when the balance of bleeding, tolerability, drug interactions, cost or concurrent anticoagulation favors it. Prasugrel additionally requires caution in older or low-weight patients: its age and weight dose considerations apply only after contraindications are excluded. Combine the selected agent with low-dose aspirin initially unless a specific alternative strategy is indicated, and reassess duration as ischemic and bleeding risks evolve. The question concerns the initial post-PCI choice, not a universal commitment to unchanged dual therapy indefinitely.

Prasugrel 60 mg loading, then 10 mg daily: This is a standard prasugrel regimen in appropriately selected PCI patients, but any previous stroke or TIA makes prasugrel unsuitable because of adverse net clinical outcomes.

Clopidogrel 600 mg loading, then 75 mg daily: Clopidogrel is a reasonable alternative when potent agents are unsuitable, bleeding risk is high or anticoagulation is required; the stated eligible PCI patient favors ticagrelor over clopidogrel.

Ticagrelor 180 mg loading, then 60 mg twice daily: The 60 mg twice-daily dose is used in selected extended secondary prevention settings after the first year; it is not the standard initial ACS maintenance dose.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

Prasugrel additionally requires caution in older or low-weight patients: its age and weight dose considerations apply only after contraindications are excluded. Combine the selected agent with low-dose aspirin initially unless a specific alternative strategy is indicated, and reassess duration as ischemic and bleeding risks evolve. The question concerns the initial post-PCI choice, not a universal commitment to unchanged dual therapy indefinitely.

Clopidogrel is a reasonable alternative when potent agents are unsuitable, bleeding risk is high or anticoagulation is required; the stated eligible PCI patient favors ticagrelor over clopidogrel.
The 60 mg twice-daily dose is used in selected extended secondary prevention settings after the first year; it is not the standard initial ACS maintenance dose.

questions.question: A 58-year-old, 82-kg patient with STEMI is proceeding directly to primary PCI without fibrinolysis. Prasugrel has been selected after contraindication screening. No P2Y12 inhibitor has been administered. Which regimen is appropriate?
options: Prasugrel 10 mg initially, followed by 10 mg daily
Prasugrel 60 mg loading, followed by 10 mg daily
Prasugrel 60 mg loading, followed by 5 mg daily
Prasugrel 30 mg loading, followed by 10 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Prasugrel Loading for Primary PCI

Correct answer: Prasugrel 60 mg loading, followed by 10 mg daily

Match the Regimen to the Reperfusion Strategy

**For eligible ACS patients undergoing PCI, prasugrel is loaded at 60 mg orally.** In a patient younger than seventy-five years and weighing at least sixty kilograms, the usual maintenance dose is ==10 mg daily==.

Exclude previous stroke or TIA and active pathological bleeding before prescribing. A contraindication cannot be corrected merely by reducing the dose.

Age at least seventy-five years or body weight below sixty kilograms requires separate caution and dose consideration; do not apply these adjustments to every patient.

Keep Primary PCI Distinct From Concurrent Fibrinolysis

**Prasugrel for primary PCI is not the standard oral adjunct administered with fibrinolysis.** Clopidogrel is used in the concurrent lytic pathway, with its own age-dependent loading approach.

Later PCI after fibrinolysis is a separate decision involving elapsed time, age, previous treatment and the selected guideline. Avoid treating a subsequent switch as permission to use any potent agent at the lytic bolus.

Check swallowing, absorption concerns and prior doses. Shock, vomiting or opioid exposure may delay oral drug effect; specialist intravenous antiplatelet treatment may be appropriate in selected circumstances. Continue bleeding surveillance and clear medication reconciliation through transfer. The choice among prasugrel, ticagrelor and clopidogrel depends on contraindications, reperfusion strategy and bleeding risk, while loading and maintenance are distinct prescribing steps. Do not mistake a correctly selected maintenance dose for adequate acute loading.

Prasugrel 10 mg initially, followed by 10 mg daily: Ten milligrams is the usual maintenance dose in this age and weight group; using it alone initially omits the loading dose needed for prompt platelet inhibition.

Prasugrel 60 mg loading, followed by 5 mg daily: Five-milligram maintenance is considered for low weight or older age with caution; neither dose-reduction feature is present in the stated patient.

Prasugrel 30 mg loading, followed by 10 mg daily: Thirty milligrams is not the standard guideline prasugrel loading regimen for this eligible primary-PCI presentation; it should not be inferred by halving another regimen.

questions.question: A 78-year-old patient receiving fibrinolysis for eligible STEMI weighs 70 kg and has a creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min. Enoxaparin is selected under its labeled STEMI regimen. Which initial schedule is appropriate?
options: No intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twelve hours
No intravenous bolus; 52.5 mg subcutaneously every twelve hours
A 30 mg intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twenty-four hours
No intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twenty-four hours
questions.explanation:
Enoxaparin When Age and Renal Adjustments Intersect

Correct answer: No intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twenty-four hours

Apply Both Adjustments to the Correct Indication

**The labeled STEMI regimen for age at least seventy-five years with creatinine clearance below thirty is 1 mg/kg subcutaneously once daily, without an intravenous bolus.** For seventy kilograms, this is ==70 mg every twenty-four hours==.

Without severe renal impairment, the older-patient STEMI regimen is 0.75 mg/kg every twelve hours without a bolus, with a seventy-five-milligram cap on each of the first two subcutaneous doses.

Do not simply combine the older-patient dose with the usual twelve-hour frequency when severe renal impairment is present. The renal table supplies the appropriate combined regimen.

Monitor Accumulation and Coordinate Subsequent Procedures

**Enoxaparin potentiates antithrombin-mediated factor Xa inhibition and has clinically important renal clearance.** Review weight, calculated creatinine clearance, blood count, platelets and bleeding before dosing.

Avoid using an indexed eGFR number interchangeably with the creatinine-clearance dosing criterion without assessing the patient and the estimation method.

Monitor changing renal function and overt or occult bleeding. Unfractionated heparin may be selected in some patients when rapid titration or reversibility is advantageous; that choice does not alter the labeled enoxaparin answer requested here. If PCI follows, document the exact last dose and time so procedural anticoagulation is selected safely. Prior heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or active major bleeding requires a different plan. Antiplatelet therapy and fibrinolytic age adjustments are separate decisions and must also be checked rather than inferred from the anticoagulant prescription.

Age <75; CrCl ≥30 mL/min | 30 mg IV, then 1 mg/kg SC every 12 h | First two SC doses maximum 100 mg each

Age ≥75; CrCl ≥30 mL/min | 0.75 mg/kg SC every 12 h | No IV bolus; first two SC doses maximum 75 mg each

Age <75; CrCl <30 mL/min: labeled STEMI regimen | 30 mg IV plus 1 mg/kg SC, then 1 mg/kg SC every 24 h | Renal adjustment changes SC frequency; initial IV bolus retained in this age group

Age ≥75; CrCl <30 mL/min | 1 mg/kg SC every 24 h | No IV bolus

UFH alternative: ACC/AHA 2025 | 60 units/kg IV then 12 units/kg/hour | Bolus maximum 4000 units; initial infusion maximum 1000 units/hour; adjust to therapeutic aPTT

No intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twelve hours: This preserves excessive dosing frequency for a creatinine clearance below thirty; omitting the bolus alone does not address renal accumulation.

No intravenous bolus; 52.5 mg subcutaneously every twelve hours: This applies the older-patient 0.75 mg/kg twice-daily regimen without making the additional severe-renal-impairment adjustment required at this creatinine clearance.

A 30 mg intravenous bolus; 70 mg subcutaneously every twenty-four hours: The once-daily renal adjustment is appropriate, but the initial intravenous bolus is omitted in STEMI patients at least seventy-five years old.

questions.question: A patient with NSTE-ACS received fondaparinux while awaiting delayed angiography. Renal function is adequate and there is no heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Angiography now identifies a lesion requiring PCI. Which anticoagulation step is appropriate?
options: Administer a procedural intravenous UFH bolus in addition to the prior fondaparinux
Proceed with fondaparinux as the sole procedural anticoagulant
Give an additional subcutaneous fondaparinux dose immediately before PCI
Start a ward-dose UFH infusion and postpone the procedural bolus until after PCI
questions.explanation:
PCI After Upstream Fondaparinux

Correct answer: Administer a procedural intravenous UFH bolus in addition to the prior fondaparinux

Recognize the Transition From Upstream Treatment to PCI

**Fondaparinux requires additional UFH when a treated NSTE-ACS patient proceeds to PCI.** The 2023 ESC guideline specifies a full-dose procedural bolus because guiding-catheter thrombosis is a concern.

Fondaparinux indirectly inhibits factor Xa through antithrombin. Its upstream efficacy does not establish that it can be used alone for every invasive procedure.

The principle is deliberate procedural supplementation, not indiscriminate switching among anticoagulants throughout admission.

Coordinate the Procedural Prescription

**Use the catheterization protocol and activated clotting-time assessment where appropriate.** Account for body weight, other anticoagulants, bleeding risk and planned glycoprotein IIb/IIIa use.

The FUTURA/OASIS-8 standard-dose strategy used UFH 85 units/kg, reduced to 60 units/kg with a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor; distinguish this trial protocol from a universal unqualified dose for all PCI situations.

Record the timing of prior fondaparinux and communicate it to the procedural team. Check renal function and contraindications before the upstream prescription and reassess if the clinical state changes. Antiplatelet treatment remains a separate component of PCI care. After an uncomplicated procedure, continued parenteral anticoagulation requires a specific indication rather than automatic continuation of every drug administered before catheterization. The key decision is to preserve appropriate upstream treatment while adding the anticoagulant coverage required for the invasive phase.

Proceed with fondaparinux as the sole procedural anticoagulant: Fondaparinux is useful upstream in selected NSTE-ACS patients, but alone it does not provide adequate catheter-related thrombotic protection during PCI.

Give an additional subcutaneous fondaparinux dose immediately before PCI: Repeating the upstream drug does not replace the recommended procedural UFH bolus and may increase bleeding without addressing the relevant procedural limitation.

Start a ward-dose UFH infusion and postpone the procedural bolus until after PCI: A UFH infusion is useful in selected upstream ACS pathways, but this patient now requires procedural anticoagulation; postponing the bolus leaves the catheterization phase inadequately covered.

ESC ACS guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehad191

FUTURA/OASIS-8 randomized trial, 2010 — https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.1320

questions.question: A 76-year-old man undergoing ACS PCI has eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73 m², hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL and normal platelets. He has no prior bleeding, stroke, malignancy or anticoagulation indication. Which ARC-HBR interpretation is correct?
options: High bleeding risk is absent because three minor criteria are required
High bleeding risk is absent because no major criterion is present
High bleeding risk is present because moderate CKD is a major criterion
High bleeding risk is present because age and moderate CKD supply two minor criteria
questions.explanation:
Recognizing High Bleeding Risk Before PCI

Correct answer: High bleeding risk is present because age and moderate CKD supply two minor criteria

Apply the Binary Consensus Framework

**ARC-HBR requires at least one major or two minor criteria at PCI.** It is not an additive point score in which every item has equal weight.

Age at least 75 years and eGFR 30–59 each constitute a minor criterion. This patient has both, despite normal hemoglobin and no bleeding history.

The conceptual one-year boundaries are BARC 3 or 5 bleeding risk at least 4%, or intracranial hemorrhage risk at least 1%; they do not predict an exact individual event probability.

Translate Risk Into a Treatment Discussion

**High bleeding risk prompts individualized prevention of bleeding while preserving coronary protection.** It does not itself prohibit PCI or justify stopping both antiplatelets.

The 2025 ACS guideline allows selected abbreviated antiplatelet strategies; timing, retained agent and ischemic risk must be specified. Treat reversible anemia, avoid unnecessary NSAIDs and assess gastrointestinal protection when appropriate.

Recheck renal function and hemoglobin during follow-up. A patient may have both high ischemic and high bleeding risk, so neither label independently dictates the complete prescription.

Selected ARC-HBR feature | Minor criterion | Major criterion

Age | ≥75 years | Age alone does not supply a major criterion

Renal function | eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m² | eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²

Hemoglobin | Men 11–12.9; women 11–11.9 g/dL | <11 g/dL

Baseline platelet count | No minor threshold in this framework | <100 × 10⁹/L

High bleeding risk is absent because three minor criteria are required: The consensus threshold is two minor criteria, not three; waiting for another abnormality would underrecognize this patient’s bleeding risk.

High bleeding risk is absent because no major criterion is present: One major criterion is sufficient but not necessary: two minor criteria also establish ARC-HBR, as in this combination of age and moderate CKD.

High bleeding risk is present because moderate CKD is a major criterion: An eGFR of 30–59 is a minor criterion; severe CKD below 30 supplies the major renal criterion, so this reaches the right label through the wrong classification.

questions.question: An ACS patient has undergone uncomplicated PCI and is preparing for discharge on aspirin plus ticagrelor. There is no high bleeding risk or oral anticoagulation indication. What is the default duration framework under the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline?
options: Plan six months of DAPT followed by aspirin alone
Plan one month of DAPT followed by aspirin alone
Plan at least twelve months of DAPT, with reassessment if the risk balance changes
Plan thirty-six months of DAPT from discharge
questions.explanation:
DAPT Duration After ACS Is a Risk-Based Prescription

Correct answer: Plan at least twelve months of DAPT, with reassessment if the risk balance changes

Begin With the ACS Default and Reassess

**The 2025 ACC/AHA default is aspirin plus an oral P2Y12 inhibitor for at least twelve months in ACS without high bleeding risk.** This addresses recurrent ischemic events as well as stent thrombosis.

Record bleeding history, anemia, renal dysfunction, concomitant drugs and anticipated procedures. Risk changes during follow-up, so the discharge plan needs explicit review.

A minimum default is not a command to continue both agents through major bleeding, nor proof that every patient benefits from extension beyond one year.

**Selected patients can transition to a different regimen without abandoning antiplatelet protection.** The agent retained and the timing matter.

For patients who have tolerated ticagrelor-based DAPT, the 2025 guideline supports ticagrelor monotherapy at least one month after PCI to reduce bleeding. This means withdrawing aspirin while continuing ticagrelor, not stopping both agents.

In high-bleeding-risk ACS PCI patients, single antiplatelet therapy after one month may be reasonable under the named framework. These strategies are not interchangeable with immediate aspirin withdrawal at the procedure, unguided early switching or a universal one-month course. Use a proton pump inhibitor when gastrointestinal bleeding risk warrants it. Explain adherence and the need to consult the treating team before interruption, especially early after stenting. A new anticoagulation indication requires its own combination strategy rather than simply adding another drug to unchanged DAPT.

Plan one month of DAPT followed by aspirin alone: An abbreviated strategy can be appropriate in selected high-bleeding-risk patients, but it is not the default for this stated lower-bleeding-risk ACS presentation.

Plan thirty-six months of DAPT from discharge: Extended treatment can benefit selected prior-MI patients with favorable ischemic-to-bleeding balance, but it requires reassessment and is not the default duration for every ACS patient.

questions.question: A patient with atrial fibrillation requiring long-term anticoagulation has uncomplicated PCI for ACS. There is no mechanical valve, significant mitral stenosis or exceptionally high stent-thrombosis risk. Under the 2025 ACC/AHA framework, which planned sequence is preferred?
options: Continue anticoagulation, aspirin and clopidogrel together for twelve months
Brief triple therapy, then stop aspirin at one to four weeks and continue anticoagulation plus clopidogrel
Stop anticoagulation after PCI and use aspirin plus clopidogrel for twelve months
Stop clopidogrel at one week and continue anticoagulation plus aspirin
questions.explanation:
Antithrombotic Therapy When AF Coexists With ACS PCI

Correct answer: Brief triple therapy, then stop aspirin at one to four weeks and continue anticoagulation plus clopidogrel

Treat Two Thrombotic Indications With the Fewest Necessary Agents

**AF-related embolic prevention and post-PCI platelet inhibition have distinct indications.** Neither DAPT nor anticoagulation alone automatically supplies all early post-ACS protection.

The 2025 ACC/AHA guideline recommends stopping aspirin after ==one to four weeks== of triple therapy, continuing an oral anticoagulant plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, preferably clopidogrel.

Choose the exact aspirin stop date according to bleeding and stent-thrombosis risks. The stated uncomplicated case does not supply a reason for prolonged triple therapy.

Preserve Appropriate Anticoagulation and Follow-Up

**For eligible AF patients, a DOAC is generally preferred over a vitamin K antagonist.** Use the indicated stroke-prevention dose with its validated renal, age, weight and interaction adjustments.

Do not substitute the low vascular-prevention rivaroxaban dose for therapeutic AF anticoagulation. Mechanical valves and significant mitral stenosis require a separate anticoagulant assessment.

Reassess hemoglobin, renal function, adherence and gastrointestinal protection. Explain which drug stops and on what date: vague instructions to reduce blood thinners can cause the wrong agent to be withdrawn. The duration of subsequent anticoagulant-plus-clopidogrel treatment is individualized, commonly through the first post-ACS year, followed by reassessment for anticoagulant monotherapy. Recurrent ischemia, bleeding or repeat intervention can change that plan. Different society frameworks use somewhat different default early aspirin windows, so attribute the one-to-four-week interval to the named guideline rather than presenting it as an identical universal rule.

Continue anticoagulation, aspirin and clopidogrel together for twelve months: Prolonged triple therapy adds substantial bleeding risk; the usual strategy limits aspirin exposure while retaining anticoagulation and a P2Y12 inhibitor.

Stop anticoagulation after PCI and use aspirin plus clopidogrel for twelve months: DAPT protects against coronary events but does not replace indicated anticoagulation for AF-related cardioembolic stroke prevention.

Stop clopidogrel at one week and continue anticoagulation plus aspirin: The recommended early aspirin-withdrawal strategy retains a P2Y12 inhibitor, preferably clopidogrel; aspirin is not the usual agent retained in its place.

questions.question: Ten days after ACS stenting, a patient on aspirin and clopidogrel develops a major upper gastrointestinal bleed. Resuscitation is underway and endoscopic hemostasis is being arranged. Which antiplatelet principle is most appropriate?
options: Stop clopidogrel for two weeks while continuing aspirin and treating the bleeding source
Withhold both antiplatelets until a repeat endoscopy documents ulcer healing
Coordinate urgently with interventional cardiology, preserve aspirin if feasible, and minimize any necessary P2Y12 interruption
Stop aspirin permanently and continue clopidogrel alone as the immediate default
questions.explanation:
Major Gastrointestinal Bleeding Soon After Coronary Stenting

Correct answer: Coordinate urgently with interventional cardiology, preserve aspirin if feasible, and minimize any necessary P2Y12 interruption

Control Hemorrhage While Recognizing Very Early Stent Risk

**Resuscitation and source control proceed urgently.** Recent coronary stenting makes antiplatelet interruption hazardous, so involve the interventional cardiologist at the same time as the endoscopy team.

The BSG/ESGE 2021 framework favors continuing DAPT when possible in patients with coronary stents. If major hemorrhage requires P2Y12 interruption, continue aspirin if feasible.

This is not an instruction to continue every agent through uncontrolled life-threatening bleeding. Severity, hemostatic success and the coronary anatomy determine the immediate individualized plan.

Write an Explicit Restart and Prevention Plan

**If still indicated, reinstate the P2Y12 inhibitor within five days under the named guidance.** This is a maximum interruption framework, not a reason to wait five days after secure hemostasis when earlier resumption is appropriate.

Assess the endoscopic lesion, recurrent bleeding risk, hemoglobin trend and coronary risk with both teams. Use appropriate proton pump inhibitor treatment and address ulcer causes.

Record the last doses, the reason for interruption, which agent continues and the intended reassessment time. A temporary hold without a restart owner can become an unintended permanent withdrawal. Heparin bridging does not replace the antiplatelet mechanism needed for a recent stent. Once stabilized, review whether the longer-term regimen can be adjusted to reduce bleeding while maintaining coronary protection. The decision is a coordinated treatment sequence rather than choosing hemorrhage or thrombosis as the only relevant danger.

Stop clopidogrel for two weeks while continuing aspirin and treating the bleeding source: Preserving aspirin can be appropriate, but a predetermined two-week P2Y12 interruption is longer than the named guideline framework for a still-indicated recent-stent agent; plan early reassessment and reinstatement.

Withhold both antiplatelets until a repeat endoscopy documents ulcer healing: Temporary interruption may be necessary in uncontrolled life-threatening hemorrhage, but requiring complete ulcer healing before resumption creates excessive early stent risk; coordinate the shortest necessary interruption after source control.

Stop aspirin permanently and continue clopidogrel alone as the immediate default: P2Y12 monotherapy is used in selected planned post-PCI strategies, but this acute major-bleeding presentation ten days after stenting requires coordinated hemostasis and individualized interruption rather than automatic permanent aspirin withdrawal.

questions.topic: Early infarct care and mechanical electrical complications
questions.question: An ACS patient has continuing ischemic discomfort, blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Tadalafil was taken eighteen hours earlier. Which immediate supportive-treatment plan is appropriate while definitive ACS care proceeds?
options: Give sublingual nitroglycerin because the current blood pressure is normal
Withhold nitrates and reassess pain and perfusion while expediting indicated coronary treatment
Use intravenous nitroglycerin because titration avoids the oral drug interaction
Give high-flow oxygen as the principal anti-ischemic treatment at the stated saturation
questions.explanation:
Recent Tadalafil Exposure During ACS

Correct answer: Withhold nitrates and reassess pain and perfusion while expediting indicated coronary treatment

Screen for Vasodilator Interactions Before Giving Nitrates

**Nitrates increase cyclic GMP, while PDE5 inhibition reduces its breakdown.** Combined exposure can produce profound hypotension despite an initially reassuring blood pressure.

The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS framework avoids nitrates within ==forty-eight hours of tadalafil==, twenty-four hours of sildenafil or vardenafil, and twelve hours of avanafil.

Also assess suspected right ventricular infarction, systolic pressure below ninety or a fall greater than thirty millimeters of mercury from baseline. Nitrate eligibility requires more than the absence of one contraindication.

Treat Persistent Ischemia Without Relying on Symptom Suppression

**Continuing ischemic discomfort requires reassessment of ECG, hemodynamics and the invasive or reperfusion plan.** Analgesia must not delay treatment of the cause.

At oxygen saturation below ninety percent, give oxygen to correct hypoxemia; routine supplemental oxygen is not recommended for the normally saturated patient described here.

Opioids may be considered selectively for severe pain unresponsive to other suitable measures, but can cause hypotension, respiratory depression and delayed absorption of oral P2Y12 drugs. Relief of pain does not prove reperfusion. When nitrates are otherwise suitable, sublingual nitroglycerin is commonly 0.3–0.4 mg every five minutes for up to three doses, with monitoring and further treatment based on response. Those usual doses remain inappropriate during the tadalafil interaction window. Record the drug and time of exposure explicitly so another clinician does not inadvertently administer a nitrate during transfer.

Give sublingual nitroglycerin because the current blood pressure is normal: Normal baseline pressure does not remove the nitrate–PDE5 inhibitor interaction; tadalafil exposure within forty-eight hours makes nitrate-associated hypotension a serious concern.

Use intravenous nitroglycerin because titration avoids the oral drug interaction: The interaction is pharmacodynamic and persists with intravenous nitrate delivery; changing the route does not remove excessive cyclic-GMP-mediated vasodilation.

Give high-flow oxygen as the principal anti-ischemic treatment at the stated saturation: Supplemental oxygen treats hypoxemia, but routine use at this normal saturation has no established benefit and does not substitute for addressing continuing coronary ischemia.

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.topic: Early infarct care and mechanical electrical complications
questions.question: After anterior MI, a patient has heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 92/64 mm Hg, cool extremities and pulmonary congestion. No beta blocker has been administered. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Give intravenous metoprolol promptly to correct the tachycardia
Defer beta-blocker initiation, treat the unstable state, and reassess after stabilization
Start low-dose oral metoprolol now with close blood-pressure monitoring
Start carvedilol now to obtain its longer-term ventricular-remodeling benefit
questions.explanation:
Defer Early Beta Blockade During Low Output

Correct answer: Defer beta-blocker initiation, treat the unstable state, and reassess after stabilization

Recognize Compensatory Tachycardia and Shock Risk

**Acute heart failure and low-output features are reasons to defer initiation of beta blockade.** A fast pulse does not establish that reducing it immediately will improve cardiac output.

Assess perfusion, congestion, ventricular function, ongoing ischemia and mechanical complications. Provide appropriate stabilization and coronary treatment.

Negative inotropy and reduced chronotropic support can worsen an already compromised circulation. Intravenous dosing does not bypass this physiological risk.

Reassess Eligibility After the Acute Contraindication Resolves

**The 2025 ACC/AHA guideline recommends early oral beta blockers in ACS without contraindications.** Begin at a low dose with cautious titration when blood pressure, perfusion and heart rate permit.

Other barriers include severe bradycardia, advanced AV block without pacing, active bronchospasm and marked PR prolongation. The traditional PR threshold is 0.24 seconds, equivalent to 240 milliseconds.

Reassess initially ineligible patients rather than documenting a permanent class prohibition. Stabilized reduced-EF heart failure is different from the acute low-output state in this stem and supports an evidence-based beta blocker when tolerated. Monitor blood pressure, pulse, congestion and conduction after initiation. The appropriate drug and titration depend on ventricular function and comorbidity. Avoid conflating this acute safety decision with the separate question of indefinite beta-blocker treatment after an uncomplicated preserved-EF infarct. The indication, timing and duration each require their own assessment.

Give intravenous metoprolol promptly to correct the tachycardia: Intravenous beta blockade can worsen low output or precipitate shock; tachycardia in this setting may be compensatory rather than an isolated treatment target.

Start low-dose oral metoprolol now with close blood-pressure monitoring: Low-dose oral initiation is appropriate after contraindications resolve, but the current low-output features and acute congestion make even cautious immediate initiation unsuitable.

Start carvedilol now to obtain its longer-term ventricular-remodeling benefit: Carvedilol benefits selected stable reduced-EF patients, but negative inotropy and vasodilation can worsen this acute hypoperfused state; long-term benefit does not remove the need for stabilization.

    • Other barriers include severe bradycardia, advanced AV block without pacing, active bronchospasm and marked PR prolongation. The traditional PR threshold is 0.24 seconds, equivalent to 240 milliseconds.
    • Reassess initially ineligible patients rather than documenting a permanent class prohibition. Stabilized reduced-EF heart failure is different from the acute low-output state in this stem and supports an evidence-based beta blocker when tolerated. Monitor blood pressure, pulse, congestion and conduction after initiation. The appropriate drug and titration depend on ventricular function and comorbidity. Avoid conflating this acute safety decision with the separate question of indefinite beta-blocker treatment after an uncomplicated preserved-EF infarct. The indication, timing and duration each require their own assessment.

Other Options

  • A — Give intravenous metoprolol promptly to correct the tachycardia: Intravenous beta blockade can worsen low output or precipitate shock; tachycardia in this setting may be compensatory rather than an isolated treatment target.
  • C — Start low-dose oral metoprolol now with close blood-pressure monitoring: Low-dose oral initiation is appropriate after contraindications resolve, but the current low-output features and acute congestion make even cautious immediate initiation unsuitable.
  • D — Start carvedilol now to obtain its longer-term ventricular-remodeling benefit: Carvedilol benefits selected stable reduced-EF patients, but negative inotropy and vasodilation can worsen this acute hypoperfused state; long-term benefit does not remove the need for stabilization.

questions.question: A stabilized patient five days after MI has LVEF 38% and diabetes, without current pulmonary congestion. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium 4.3 mmol/L. An ACE inhibitor and appropriate beta blocker are tolerated. Which additional treatment is supported?
options: Withhold an MRA because heart-failure symptoms are absent today
Add eplerenone with potassium and renal-function monitoring
Replace the ACE inhibitor with eplerenone rather than combining them
Replace the ACE inhibitor with sacubitril–valsartan as the preferred post-MI addition
questions.explanation:
Mineralocorticoid Antagonism After MI With Diabetes

Correct answer: Add eplerenone with potassium and renal-function monitoring

Use the Post-Infarct Eligibility Framework

**After MI, LVEF at most forty percent with heart failure or diabetes supports mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism when safe.** Absence of congestion at this examination does not exclude the diabetic patient described here.

Eplerenone blocks aldosterone-mediated sodium retention and adverse remodeling. Its benefit is additional to other indicated post-infarct therapy.

Assess hemodynamic stability and review renal function, potassium and interacting drugs before initiation rather than selecting treatment from EF alone.

Initiate Safely and Recheck Laboratory Results

**Under the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA safety framework, initiate an MRA when eGFR is greater than thirty and potassium below 5.0.** The question’s values satisfy these boundaries.

With adequate renal function, start eplerenone at ==25 mg daily== and titrate toward ==50 mg daily==, preferably within four weeks if tolerated. Reduced renal function can require a lower starting schedule.

Measure potassium before treatment, within the first week and one month after initiation or dose adjustment, then periodically. Review renal function alongside potassium and recheck during dehydration, acute illness or interacting-drug changes. Avoid unnecessary potassium supplements and review NSAIDs and other potassium-raising medicines. Strong CYP3A inhibitors are contraindicated with eplerenone; moderate inhibitors can require dose limitation. Continue indicated ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy with monitoring rather than combining an ACE inhibitor and ARB. Persistent hyperkalemia requires dose adjustment or withdrawal according to the treatment protocol.

Withhold an MRA because heart-failure symptoms are absent today: Post-MI diabetes with LVEF at most forty percent supports MRA treatment even without current HF symptoms, provided renal function and potassium permit.

Replace the ACE inhibitor with eplerenone rather than combining them: An MRA complements tolerated renin–angiotensin inhibition in eligible patients; it is not a routine substitute for the ACE inhibitor solely to avoid combination treatment.

Replace the ACE inhibitor with sacubitril–valsartan as the preferred post-MI addition: Sacubitril–valsartan has an established role in appropriate symptomatic HFrEF, but PARADISE-MI did not demonstrate significant superiority over ramipril for its primary endpoint after acute MI; it does not replace the specific additional MRA indication here.

questions.topic: Early infarct care and mechanical electrical complications
questions.question: Three days after inferior MI, a patient abruptly develops pulmonary edema and shock. A soft apical systolic murmur is heard. Echocardiography shows a flail mitral leaflet with a mobile attached subvalvular structure and severe eccentric regurgitation; no septal shunt is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Post-infarct ventricular septal rupture
Ischemic leaflet tethering from ventricular remodeling
Papillary muscle rupture causing acute severe mitral regurgitation
Dynamic outflow obstruction with systolic anterior mitral motion
questions.explanation:
Papillary Muscle Rupture After Inferior MI

Correct answer: Papillary muscle rupture causing acute severe mitral regurgitation

Recognize Acute Structural Mitral Failure

**Papillary muscle rupture causes abrupt severe MR, pulmonary edema and circulatory collapse.** The posteromedial muscle is particularly vulnerable because its arterial supply is usually less redundant.

A loud murmur is not required: rapid left ventricular–atrial pressure equalization can make the murmur short or soft despite catastrophic regurgitation.

Transthoracic echocardiography is urgent. Use transesophageal imaging when the mechanism or severity is inadequately defined, without allowing additional imaging to delay necessary stabilization and surgical coordination.

Stabilize as a Bridge to Definitive Treatment

**Activate cardiac surgery and the shock team immediately.** Acute rupture is a surgical emergency, commonly requiring mitral replacement; selected partial ruptures may be repairable.

Support oxygenation and perfusion. Afterload reduction may help when pressure permits, while hypotension requires individualized vasoactive and mechanical-support decisions.

Temporary mechanical support may bridge a selected patient to surgery, but is not definitive treatment for the disrupted valve apparatus. Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is a specialized alternative in selected prohibitive-risk patients rather than a universal replacement for surgery. Distinguish structural rupture from functional ischemic MR because their mechanisms and procedural decisions differ. Reassess coronary anatomy and the need for concomitant revascularization with the surgical team. Do not attribute sudden post-infarct edema solely to infarct size when the clinical course suggests a mechanical event.

Post-infarct ventricular septal rupture: Septal rupture produces an interventricular left-to-right shunt, often with a harsh parasternal murmur; imaging here demonstrates mitral apparatus disruption without that shunt.

Ischemic leaflet tethering from ventricular remodeling: Functional ischemic MR results from altered ventricular geometry and leaflet restriction; an acutely flail leaflet with an attached disrupted subvalvular structure supports rupture instead.

Dynamic outflow obstruction with systolic anterior mitral motion: Dynamic obstruction can cause shock and MR, but echocardiography would show systolic anterior motion and an outflow gradient rather than a flail apparatus from rupture.

AHA scientific statement on mechanical complications of MI, 2021 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9364424/

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.topic: Early infarct care and mechanical electrical complications
questions.question: Four days after MI, a patient develops hypotension and a new harsh left parasternal systolic murmur with a thrill. Oxygen saturation rises from 61% in the right atrium to 82% in the right ventricle. Which complication best explains these findings?
options: Left ventricular free-wall rupture with tamponade
Papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation
Ventricular septal rupture with left-to-right shunting
Isolated right ventricular infarction
questions.explanation:
Shunt Physiology in Post-Infarct Septal Rupture

Correct answer: Ventricular septal rupture with left-to-right shunting

Localize the Abnormal Flow

**A new ventricular-level oxygen saturation step-up indicates entry of oxygenated blood into the right ventricle.** In this post-infarct setting, the murmur and hemodynamic deterioration strongly support septal rupture.

The left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary flow and RV volume burden while reducing effective systemic output. Infarct-related dysfunction can compound the shock.

Urgent echocardiography with color Doppler defines the defect, shunt, ventricular function and associated valve or pericardial abnormalities. Catheter data can support physiology but must not delay an already urgent diagnosis.

Coordinate Closure and Stabilization

**Activate cardiac surgery and the shock team promptly.** Definitive treatment generally requires closure; medical support alone does not repair the structural defect.

Refractory shock or pulmonary edema requires urgent intervention. In selected stabilized patients, timing can be individualized to balance ongoing shunt risk against friable infarct tissue.

Do not claim that all patients must wait a fixed number of weeks: apparent advantages of delayed surgery in observational cohorts are affected by survival and selection bias. Temporary mechanical support may provide a bridge in selected patients, with device choice guided by shunt physiology and ventricular function. Percutaneous closure is an option in selected anatomy, residual defects or patients unsuitable for surgery, requiring specialist assessment. Communicate whether instability is persistent or controlled, because that distinction determines whether a bridging strategy is feasible. The oxygen step-up identifies the mechanism; the patient’s trajectory determines urgency.

Complication | Key physiology | Urgent imaging clue

Septal rupture | LV-to-RV shunt; ventricular oxygen step-up | Color Doppler flow across disrupted septum

Papillary muscle rupture | Acute MR; pulmonary venous hypertension | Flail mitral apparatus and severe often eccentric MR

Free-wall rupture | Hemopericardium; tamponade; possible PEA | Pericardial blood/clot with compressive physiology

Left ventricular free-wall rupture with tamponade: Free-wall rupture causes hemopericardium and impaired filling, often with collapse or PEA; it does not produce a ventricular-level oxygen saturation step-up.

Papillary muscle rupture with acute mitral regurgitation: Acute MR causes pulmonary venous hypertension and edema, but does not directly introduce oxygenated LV blood into the right ventricle to produce the stated step-up.

Isolated right ventricular infarction: RV infarction can cause hypotension and elevated venous pressure, but does not create a new LV-to-RV shunt with a harsh thrill-producing murmur.

questions.topic: Early infarct care and mechanical electrical complications
questions.question: Five days after MI, a patient suddenly collapses with pulseless electrical activity. During resuscitation, bedside echocardiography shows a new echodense pericardial collection with chamber compression. What is the most likely complication?
options: Ventricular septal rupture causing an acute intracardiac shunt
Ventricular free-wall rupture causing hemopericardium and tamponade
Papillary muscle rupture causing acute mitral regurgitation
Isolated recurrent infarction causing primary pump failure
questions.explanation:
Free-Wall Rupture With Hemopericardium

Correct answer: Ventricular free-wall rupture causing hemopericardium and tamponade

Recognize a Mechanical Cause of Pulseless Electrical Activity

**Post-infarct free-wall rupture can rapidly fill the pericardium with blood and cause tamponade.** The resulting obstruction to filling can produce PEA despite electrical activity.

Bedside echocardiography may show pericardial fluid or clot and compressive physiology; direct visualization of the tear is not necessary to trigger urgent concern.

Continue resuscitation while activating cardiac surgery. An echodense collection may contain clot, so the absence of a large simple fluid pocket does not exclude hemopericardium.

Prioritize Definitive Repair and Individualized Rescue

**Suspected free-wall rupture with tamponade requires emergency surgical management.** Drainage alone does not repair the bleeding ventricular wall.

If surgery cannot be reached immediately and the patient cannot survive without decompression, controlled limited drainage may be used by an experienced team as a bridge. Rapid complete decompression can aggravate bleeding.

Avoid treating this as an uncomplicated inflammatory effusion or delaying surgery to obtain elective cross-sectional imaging in a collapsing patient. Selected temporary circulatory support may assist rescue, although tamponade can limit venous drainage and device flow. A contained rupture can later form a pseudoaneurysm, whose wall lacks normal full-thickness myocardium and requires separate specialist assessment. Do not infer safety from temporary hemodynamic improvement: the structural lesion remains. Communicate the post-infarct timing, arrest rhythm and bedside findings immediately so transfer and definitive treatment proceed together.

Ventricular septal rupture causing an acute intracardiac shunt: Septal rupture can produce shock, but its defining imaging feature is interventricular flow rather than a new compressive pericardial blood collection.

Papillary muscle rupture causing acute mitral regurgitation: Acute MR causes pulmonary edema and shock with mitral apparatus disruption; it does not account for the newly demonstrated hemopericardium.

Isolated recurrent infarction causing primary pump failure: Reinfarction can cause collapse, but the new pericardial collection and compression identify an additional mechanical explanation requiring immediate treatment.

explanationTeaching.title: Free-Wall Rupture With Hemopericardium

sections.heading: Recognize a Mechanical Cause of Pulseless Electrical Activity

bullets.text: **Post-infarct free-wall rupture can rapidly fill the pericardium with blood and cause tamponade.** The resulting obstruction to filling can produce PEA despite electrical activity.
children: Bedside echocardiography may show pericardial fluid or clot and compressive physiology; direct visualization of the tear is not necessary to trigger urgent concern.
Continue resuscitation while activating cardiac surgery. An echodense collection may contain clot, so the absence of a large simple fluid pocket does not exclude hemopericardium.

sections.heading: Prioritize Definitive Repair and Individualized Rescue

bullets.text: **Suspected free-wall rupture with tamponade requires emergency surgical management.** Drainage alone does not repair the bleeding ventricular wall.
children: If surgery cannot be reached immediately and the patient cannot survive without decompression, controlled limited drainage may be used by an experienced team as a bridge. Rapid complete decompression can aggravate bleeding.

Avoid treating this as an uncomplicated inflammatory effusion or delaying surgery to obtain elective cross-sectional imaging in a collapsing patient. Selected temporary circulatory support may assist rescue, although tamponade can limit venous drainage and device flow. A contained rupture can later form a pseudoaneurysm, whose wall lacks normal full-thickness myocardium and requires separate specialist assessment. Do not infer safety from temporary hemodynamic improvement: the structural lesion remains. Communicate the post-infarct timing, arrest rhythm and bedside findings immediately so transfer and definitive treatment proceed together.

otherOptions.explanation: Septal rupture can produce shock, but its defining imaging feature is interventricular flow rather than a new compressive pericardial blood collection.
Acute MR causes pulmonary edema and shock with mitral apparatus disruption; it does not account for the newly demonstrated hemopericardium.
Reinfarction can cause collapse, but the new pericardial collection and compression identify an additional mechanical explanation requiring immediate treatment.

questions.topic: Early infarct care and mechanical electrical complications
questions.question: Six hours after STEMI, a monitored patient suddenly becomes unresponsive and pulseless. The monitor shows ventricular fibrillation and a defibrillator is immediately available. Which action has priority?
options: Deliver prompt unsynchronized defibrillation with high-quality CPR and the cardiac-arrest pathway
Give intravenous amiodarone before the first shock
Perform synchronized cardioversion after establishing a stable synchronization marker
Correct potassium before attempting electrical treatment
questions.explanation:
Early VF Requires Resuscitation and Trigger Assessment

Correct answer: Deliver prompt unsynchronized defibrillation with high-quality CPR and the cardiac-arrest pathway

Treat the Arrest Before Classifying Its Long-Term Implications

**VF is a shockable cardiac-arrest rhythm.** Provide prompt defibrillation and high-quality CPR with minimal interruption, following the current resuscitation algorithm.

In the AHA 2025 shockable pathway, epinephrine begins during CPR after the second shock; amiodarone or lidocaine is considered after the third. Resume CPR immediately after each shock for two minutes before rhythm reassessment, minimizing pauses. Drug preparation must not delay defibrillation.

Assess reversible causes during resuscitation, including hypoxia, electrolyte disturbance and coronary ischemia, without prolonged pauses for testing.

Reassess Ischemia and Recurrence After Circulation Returns

**Early timing does not make a ventricular arrhythmia harmless.** Evaluate reperfusion, recurrent occlusion, hemodynamics, ventricular function, potassium, magnesium and drug-related proarrhythmia.

Recurrent malignant arrhythmias may require antiarrhythmic therapy and sympathetic control when hemodynamically suitable, alongside treatment of the ischemic substrate.

A transient early infarct-related arrhythmia does not by itself establish an immediate permanent ICD indication. Later sustained VT/VF or an event without a reversible explanation requires secondary-prevention assessment. Distinguish VF from nonsustained VT and tolerated reperfusion rhythms; routine prophylactic antiarrhythmics are not justified merely by an infarct diagnosis.

AHA 2025 adult VF/pVT arrest intervention | Dose or delivery | Qualification

Biphasic defibrillation | Manufacturer recommendation, e.g. 120–200 J initially; maximum available if unknown | Subsequent shocks equivalent or higher energy as appropriate

Epinephrine IV/IO | 1 mg every 3–5 minutes | After initial defibrillation attempts in the shockable pathway

Amiodarone IV/IO | 300 mg bolus, then 150 mg if needed | For shock-refractory VF/pVT

CPR | 100–120 compressions/min; adult depth at least 5 cm, avoiding >6 cm | Full recoil, minimal interruption and appropriate ventilation

Give intravenous amiodarone before the first shock: Amiodarone may be considered for shock-refractory VF, but administering it first must not delay prompt defibrillation of a witnessed shockable arrest.

Perform synchronized cardioversion after establishing a stable synchronization marker: Synchronization is used for selected organized tachyarrhythmias with a pulse; VF has no reliable QRS target and requires unsynchronized defibrillation.

Correct potassium before attempting electrical treatment: Electrolyte abnormalities require correction during resuscitation, but laboratory confirmation or replacement must not delay the first shock for VF.

questions.topic: Early infarct care and mechanical electrical complications
questions.question: During inferior STEMI, complete AV block occurs with a narrow-complex escape at 48/min and preserved perfusion. After successful reperfusion, normal AV conduction returns and remains stable without bundle-branch block. What is the appropriate pacing approach?
options: Insert a transvenous temporary pacemaker during the post-reperfusion observation period
Schedule permanent pacing on day five based on the documented complete block
Continue monitored reassessment without automatic permanent pacemaker implantation
Schedule permanent pacing on day ten even if normal conduction is maintained
questions.explanation:
Transient AV Block After Inferior Infarction

Correct answer: Continue monitored reassessment without automatic permanent pacemaker implantation

Infer the Likely Level of Block Without Treating It as Certain

**AV block accompanying inferior MI is commonly nodal or supra-Hisian and can resolve after reperfusion.** A narrow escape supports this mechanism but does not replace assessment of symptoms and stability.

Anterior MI with new intraventricular conduction disease more often indicates infra-Hisian injury, an unreliable wide escape and a larger infarct burden.

Review drugs, electrolytes and recurrent ischemia. Avoid unnecessary AV-nodal suppression while clinically important block is present.

Separate Temporary Support From Permanent Device Indication

**Refractory symptoms or hemodynamic compromise can require temporary pacing.** Atropine may help vagally mediated or nodal block, but should not delay pacing when ineffective in an unstable patient.

ESC 2021 describes individualized observation for persistent block, commonly five to ten days; if it has not resolved within ten days, permanent pacing should be performed. Earlier consideration depends on factors including unsuccessful or late reperfusion, anterior MI, preceding bifascicular/AV block and progression. This waiting framework concerns unresolved block, not the recovered conduction in this stem.

Assess escape reliability and clinical deterioration throughout observation; temporary support can be needed while recovery is awaited. When a permanent device is indicated, ventricular function and anticipated pacing burden influence selection of conventional pacing, resynchronization or an ICD-capable system. Stable recovery after reperfusion supports monitored reassessment rather than implantation based solely on the earlier complete-block tracing.

Insert a transvenous temporary pacemaker during the post-reperfusion observation period: Temporary pacing is appropriate for refractory symptomatic bradycardia or hemodynamic compromise, but adds invasive risk without a current indication when conduction and perfusion have recovered.

Schedule permanent pacing on day five based on the documented complete block: A five-day assessment interval can apply to unresolved infarct-related block, but the previous rhythm alone does not create a device indication after stable recovery.

Schedule permanent pacing on day ten even if normal conduction is maintained: Ten days is an upper observation boundary for unresolved block in the ESC discussion, not a scheduled device indication for a patient whose conduction has recovered.

questions.topic: Post-infarct recovery and secondary prevention
questions.question: After anterior MI and PCI, contrast echocardiography confirms an apical LV thrombus. The patient has no active bleeding. Under the AHA 2022 statement, which management framework is appropriate?
options: Give anticoagulation for one week and stop when symptoms resolve
Continue DAPT alone and repeat imaging at three months
Prescribe indefinite anticoagulation without planned repeat imaging
Begin oral anticoagulation, typically for three months, with repeat imaging and a coordinated antiplatelet plan
questions.explanation:
Confirmed LV Thrombus After Anterior MI

Correct answer: Begin oral anticoagulation, typically for three months, with repeat imaging and a coordinated antiplatelet plan

Treat Confirmed Thrombus Rather Than Inferring Protection From DAPT

**Post-MI LV thrombus generally warrants oral anticoagulation.** The AHA 2022 statement describes a typical duration of ==three months==, followed by reassessment rather than an automatic stop regardless of findings.

Apical akinesis, endocardial injury and blood stasis after a large anterior infarct promote thrombus formation. Embolism can occur without warning symptoms.

Warfarin is an established option; the statement considers a DOAC a reasonable alternative on available evidence. Select the drug and dose using renal function, interactions, adherence and the patient’s other indications.

Use Imaging and Bleeding Risk to Guide the Next Decision

**Repeat imaging assesses resolution and ventricular recovery.** Contrast echocardiography improves apical definition, while CMR is useful when echocardiography is inconclusive or clinical suspicion remains high.

Persistent thrombus requires assessment of morphology, anticoagulant exposure and adherence before deciding whether to extend or change therapy.

Coordinate the coronary antiplatelet regimen because adding anticoagulation to DAPT increases bleeding. Avoid leaving three agents unchanged indefinitely without an explicit indication and review date. Document the planned imaging modality, timing and clinician responsible for reviewing the result. Prophylactic anticoagulation for apical akinesis without demonstrated thrombus is a different, less certain decision and should not be equated with treatment of confirmed thrombus. The evidence-based duration framework must remain linked to the actual imaging and clinical course.

Give anticoagulation for one week and stop when symptoms resolve: A short symptomatic course is not an adequate treatment framework for confirmed LV thrombus; embolic risk and thrombus resolution cannot be inferred from relief of infarct symptoms.

Continue DAPT alone and repeat imaging at three months: DAPT is important after coronary stenting but does not replace indicated anticoagulation for confirmed LV thrombus; waiting for surveillance imaging leaves systemic embolic risk untreated.

Prescribe indefinite anticoagulation without planned repeat imaging: Persistent thrombus or another indication can justify prolonged anticoagulation, but duration should be reassessed using resolution, ventricular recovery and bleeding rather than prescribed indefinitely without imaging.
