questions.topic: Post-infarct recovery and secondary prevention
questions.question: Three weeks after MI, a patient develops fever, pleuritic positional chest pain, a pericardial rub, elevated CRP and a small pleuropericardial effusion. There is no new troponin rise, territorial ECG evolution or echocardiographic evidence of rupture. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Early infarct-associated pericarditis from adjacent myocardial necrosis
Dressler syndrome within the post-cardiac injury syndrome spectrum
Recurrent myocardial infarction
Contained ventricular free-wall rupture
questions.explanation:
Delayed Inflammatory Pericarditis After MI

Correct answer: Dressler syndrome within the post-cardiac injury syndrome spectrum

Use Timing Together With Inflammatory Evidence

**Dressler syndrome is delayed post-MI pericarditis within the post-cardiac injury syndrome spectrum.** Timing varies; a latency of weeks and pleuropericardial inflammation support an immune-mediated process.

Early infarct-associated pericarditis occurs in the first days and reflects local injury. Timing alone is insufficient without compatible symptoms, examination and investigations.

Assess ECG, serial troponin when appropriate, inflammatory markers and echocardiography. New hypotension, a substantial effusion or an atypical course requires renewed evaluation for rupture, tamponade or another cause.

Treat Inflammation Without Overlooking Coronary Therapy

**The 2025 ESC guideline favors high-dose aspirin as the anti-inflammatory agent after MI**, with colchicine when suitable. Coordinate the prescription with the existing antiplatelet regimen and bleeding risk.

The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS dosing table lists aspirin 500–1000 mg every six to eight hours until improvement and colchicine 0.5–0.6 mg once or twice daily for three months. Use once-daily colchicine below seventy kilograms, with further renal, hepatic and interaction adjustments. Provide gastroprotection and coordinate high-dose aspirin with the existing antiplatelet regimen; these anti-inflammatory doses differ from routine maintenance aspirin.

The guideline describes a short five-to-seven-day aspirin course with colchicine as reasonable for early post-MI pericarditis; delayed inflammatory disease requires duration and tapering guided by response. Corticosteroids are not routine first-line treatment when aspirin and colchicine are suitable. Reassess symptoms, CRP and effusion, and investigate alternative diagnoses if improvement is inadequate. A new post-infarct pain episode must first be evaluated rather than labeled Dressler syndrome simply because several weeks have elapsed.

Early infarct-associated pericarditis from adjacent myocardial necrosis: Early pericarditis usually occurs in the first days after infarction; the delayed inflammatory pleuropericardial presentation favors the immune-mediated syndrome.

Recurrent myocardial infarction: Reinfarction requires renewed ischemic assessment and supporting acute injury evidence; the stated pain pattern, rub and inflammatory effusions without new ischemic findings favor pericarditis.

Contained ventricular free-wall rupture: A contained rupture can present subacutely and must be excluded, but structural disruption or a pseudoaneurysmal cavity rather than this inflammatory syndrome would support that diagnosis.

questions.question: After an inferior MI, imaging shows an inferolateral ventricular outpouching with an abrupt myocardial discontinuity and a narrow communication. The sac wall consists of adherent pericardial tissue rather than a continuous myocardial scar. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Loculated pericardial effusion without ventricular rupture
True post-infarct ventricular aneurysm
Congenital muscular ventricular diverticulum
Left ventricular pseudoaneurysm
questions.explanation:
Contained Rupture Versus True Ventricular Aneurysm

Correct answer: Left ventricular pseudoaneurysm

Identify the Wall Composition and Communication

**A pseudoaneurysm is a contained ventricular rupture.** Pericardium, adhesions and thrombotic material contain the sac rather than an intact myocardial wall.

A narrow neck and inferior or lateral location are useful clues, but neck geometry alone is not an infallible diagnostic rule.

Echocardiography evaluates flow and ventricular function; CMR or cardiac CT can clarify wall continuity and surrounding tissue when the patient is stable enough for further imaging.

Connect the Diagnosis to Management Urgency

**Pseudoaneurysm requires prompt surgical or structural-heart assessment because rupture risk differs from that of a mature true aneurysm.** Instability or evidence of ongoing rupture requires emergency treatment.

An incidentally identified chronic lesion after remote MI may permit urgent planned assessment rather than immediate emergency surgery. Anatomy, symptoms, expansion and operative risk inform the decision.

True aneurysms more often cause chronic heart failure, ventricular arrhythmia or thrombus-related embolism. Their management includes appropriate ventricular therapy and anticoagulation when indicated; surgery is reserved for selected refractory complications or associated operative indications. Do not prescribe automatic surgery for every stable true aneurysm, or reassurance for a pseudoaneurysm simply because the rupture is currently contained. Document whether the wall contains myocardial scar, the communication, sac dimensions, thrombus and interval change. Those findings provide a stronger basis for decision-making than the nonspecific word aneurysm alone.

Loculated pericardial effusion without ventricular rupture: A loculated effusion lies outside the ventricle without the demonstrated communication through disrupted ventricular myocardium into an outpouching.

True post-infarct ventricular aneurysm: A true aneurysm represents expansion of scarred ventricular wall with myocardial continuity, usually with a broader transition; the described contained wall disruption favors pseudoaneurysm.

Congenital muscular ventricular diverticulum: A muscular diverticulum contains myocardial tissue and typically contracts with the ventricle; it does not explain the acquired post-infarct wall discontinuity and pericardial sac.

questions.topic: Post-infarct recovery and secondary prevention
questions.question: Ten days after MI and successful PCI, a stable patient has LVEF 28%. There has been no sustained VT or VF, and ventricular therapy has just been initiated. Which device strategy is appropriate?
options: Implant a primary-prevention ICD before discharge using the current EF
Optimize medical therapy and reassess EF after the post-MI and post-revascularization recovery intervals
Recheck EF at six weeks and implant then if it remains twenty-eight percent
Continue medical therapy and reserve device assessment for a future sustained VT episode
questions.explanation:
Reassess EF Before Primary-Prevention ICD Implantation

Correct answer: Optimize medical therapy and reassess EF after the post-MI and post-revascularization recovery intervals

Distinguish Early Risk From a Proven Device Indication

**Primary-prevention ICD implantation is not routinely performed within forty days after MI.** An early low EF may reflect stunning and evolving remodeling as well as permanent injury.

The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA framework supports EF reassessment beyond forty days after MI and beyond ninety days after revascularization or medical optimization when determining device candidacy.

The patient has no separate secondary-prevention arrhythmic indication. Do not apply the primary-prevention waiting framework mechanically to every survivor of sustained VT or VF without evaluating reversibility.

Assess Persistent Eligibility and Competing Risks

**Later candidacy requires persistent ventricular dysfunction despite appropriate therapy and a meaningful survival expectation exceeding one year.** Symptoms and EF thresholds matter.

In the named framework, ischemic disease with EF at most thirty-five percent and NYHA II–III symptoms supports an ICD when other criteria are satisfied; selected NYHA I post-MI patients qualify at EF at most thirty percent.

Repeat ventricular imaging and review treatment tolerance, comorbidity and patient preferences. Assess QRS morphology and duration if resynchronization may be relevant. A wearable defibrillator is a separate individualized bridging decision, not an automatic proven substitute for every patient awaiting reassessment. Explain the recovery plan and arrange a definite review so appropriate delay does not become indefinite omission of device assessment. The purpose is to select patients with a persistent, evidence-supported benefit rather than implant from a single acute-phase measurement.

Implant a primary-prevention ICD before discharge using the current EF: A severely reduced early EF identifies risk but can improve; routine primary-prevention implantation during the first forty days after MI has not improved overall prognosis.

Recheck EF at six weeks and implant then if it remains twenty-eight percent: Six weeks exceeds the post-MI interval, but recent revascularization and newly initiated therapy also require recovery and reassessment; that date is too early for the routine pathway described here.

Continue medical therapy and reserve device assessment for a future sustained VT episode: Secondary prevention follows an arrhythmic event, but eligible persistent ventricular dysfunction can justify primary-prevention assessment without waiting for sustained VT or VF.

questions.topic: Post-infarct recovery and secondary prevention
questions.question: Six weeks after ACS, a patient taking maximally tolerated atorvastatin 80 mg daily has LDL-C 86 mg/dL with confirmed adherence. Triglycerides are 130 mg/dL. Under the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS framework, which next step is appropriate?
options: Add a fibrate as the preferred response to the residual LDL elevation
Continue the same regimen because LDL-C is already below 100 mg/dL
Replace atorvastatin with a moderate-intensity statin before considering combination therapy
Add an evidence-based nonstatin LDL-lowering agent while continuing the tolerated statin
questions.explanation:
Nonstatin Escalation After ACS

Correct answer: Add an evidence-based nonstatin LDL-lowering agent while continuing the tolerated statin

Use the Named Guideline’s Escalation Threshold

**The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline recommends adding a nonstatin when LDL-C remains at least seventy mg/dL on maximally tolerated statin therapy.** At fifty-five to sixty-nine, addition is reasonable.

High-intensity statin treatment remains the foundation when tolerated. A numerically improved LDL does not establish that residual risk has been adequately addressed.

Reassess adherence, drug access, interactions and secondary causes before labeling treatment failure. The six-week measurement is within the recommended four-to-eight-week follow-up interval.

Select Additional Therapy According to Required Reduction

**Ezetimibe and PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies are established options with cardiovascular outcome evidence.** Selection depends on the magnitude of lowering needed, prior therapy, tolerance and access.

Ezetimibe is commonly prescribed at ten milligrams daily. A PCSK9 antibody can provide a larger additional reduction when the remaining LDL burden warrants it.

Distinguish an escalation threshold from a treatment goal. The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline recommends LDL-C below 55 mg/dL and non-HDL-C below 85 mg/dL for very-high-risk secondary prevention; ASCVD patients outside that category generally have an LDL-C goal below 70 mg/dL, with further intensification toward below 55 reasonable in selected patients. Continue lifestyle treatment and reassess response. Avoid reducing a tolerated statin merely because combination treatment achieves a low LDL. Explain the additional agent and arrange a documented follow-up lipid measurement.

Framework | Value | Meaning

ACC/AHA ACS 2025 | LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL on maximal tolerated statin | Add a nonstatin

ACC/AHA ACS 2025 | LDL-C 55–69 mg/dL on maximal tolerated statin | Nonstatin addition is reasonable

ACC/AHA dyslipidemia 2026: very-high-risk ASCVD | LDL-C <55; non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL | Secondary-prevention treatment goals

ACC/AHA ACS 2025 | 4–8 weeks | Reassess lipid profile after discharge

ESC ACS 2023 | LDL-C <55 mg/dL and ≥50% reduction from baseline | Post-ACS treatment goals

ESC ACS 2023 | 4–6 weeks after treatment adjustment | Reassess response; add ezetimibe then PCSK9 inhibitor if goals remain unmet

Add a fibrate as the preferred response to the residual LDL elevation: Fibrates have selected triglyceride-related uses, but the stated normal triglycerides and residual LDL burden favor an LDL-directed outcome-supported nonstatin.

Continue the same regimen because LDL-C is already below 100 mg/dL: A threshold of one hundred does not reflect the named post-ACS escalation framework; LDL-C at least seventy on maximal statin treatment supports adding a nonstatin.

Replace atorvastatin with a moderate-intensity statin before considering combination therapy: Dose reduction is appropriate for intolerance or another specific reason, but the patient tolerates high-intensity treatment and needs additional LDL lowering.

questions.topic: Post-infarct recovery and secondary prevention
questions.question: A stable patient is ready for discharge after ACS PCI. The nearest center-based rehabilitation program is difficult to reach. Which discharge approach is most appropriate?
options: Arrange comprehensive rehabilitation referral now and assess a suitable home-based or hybrid program
Reassess rehabilitation referral at the six-week clinic visit after initial recovery
Provide a walking plan and written prevention advice as the complete discharge program
Refer to the distant center-based program without assessing alternative delivery
questions.explanation:
Rehabilitation Referral Before ACS Discharge

Correct answer: Arrange comprehensive rehabilitation referral now and assess a suitable home-based or hybrid program

Prescribe a Comprehensive Recovery Program

**Refer eligible ACS patients to cardiac rehabilitation before discharge.** The program combines graduated exercise, risk-factor management, medication support, nutrition and psychosocial care.

Assess ventricular function, residual ischemia, rhythm problems and functional capacity to determine suitable training and supervision.

A successful PCI does not remove the need for prevention and recovery support. The treatment target includes function, adherence and recurrent-event risk, not merely the treated lesion.

Address Access and Tobacco Use Explicitly

**Home-based or hybrid rehabilitation can improve access for selected patients.** Selection still requires assessment; evidence and safety should not be assumed identical for every high-risk presentation.

Ask about transport, cost, work, caregiving and digital access. Give a concrete contact and appointment plan rather than a generic instruction to exercise.

For tobacco use, combine behavioral support with appropriate cessation pharmacotherapy after reviewing contraindications and patient preferences. Address secondhand exposure and arrange follow-up for relapse rather than treating a single bedside warning as a complete intervention. Provide individualized advice on activity progression, return to work and recognition of recurrent ischemic symptoms. Medication access and adherence should be reviewed alongside rehabilitation enrollment. A referral alone is not evidence that the patient attended, so follow-up should confirm participation and address barriers. The appropriate response to travel difficulty is a feasible supervised recovery pathway, not omission of care.

Reassess rehabilitation referral at the six-week clinic visit after initial recovery: Later review can refine training and barriers, but referral before discharge improves the opportunity to connect eligible patients with recovery services; stability does not require a six-week delay in referral.

Provide a walking plan and written prevention advice as the complete discharge program: Walking and written advice can support recovery, but do not supply the assessment, graduated training, medication support and psychosocial components of comprehensive rehabilitation.

Refer to the distant center-based program without assessing alternative delivery: Center-based rehabilitation is effective when accessible, but an unaddressed travel barrier can prevent participation; suitable home-based or hybrid delivery should be assessed rather than relying on an impractical referral.

questions.topic: Post-infarct recovery and secondary prevention
questions.question: A clinician reviews contemporary randomized evidence for routine long-term beta blockers after an uncomplicated MI in patients with LVEF at least 50% and no other beta-blocker indication. Which interpretation is best supported by the 2025 individual-patient meta-analysis?
options: The findings support avoiding beta blockers during the acute admission as well as follow-up
Routine treatment established a mortality benefit equivalent to that in reduced-EF heart failure
Routine treatment did not reduce the composite of death, MI or heart failure in the preserved-EF population studied
The findings establish noninferiority of withdrawal in patients already receiving long-term treatment
questions.explanation:
Long-Term Beta Blockers With Preserved EF

Correct answer: Routine treatment did not reduce the composite of death, MI or heart failure in the preserved-EF population studied

Specify the EF Group and Clinical Question

**The 2025 individual-patient meta-analysis pooled contemporary trials in post-MI patients with LVEF at least fifty percent.** Routine beta blockers did not lower the composite of all-cause death, MI or heart failure.

This result should not be extended unchanged to EF forty to forty-nine percent, established HF, symptomatic angina, arrhythmia or another independent indication.

Distinguish long-term event prevention from the acute hemodynamic and antiarrhythmic decisions made during the infarct admission.

Separate Treatment Initiation From Withdrawal

**ABYSS studied interruption versus continuation in patients already receiving long-term beta blockers.** Failure to demonstrate noninferiority of interruption prevents a blanket claim that withdrawal is equivalent.

Trials differ in EF entry criteria, endpoints and time since MI. A broad statement that all modern trials prove the same result obscures those clinically important differences.

Review ventricular function, blood pressure, angina, rhythm, adverse effects and the original indication before changing an established prescription. If discontinuation is selected, use a supervised taper rather than an automatic abrupt stop. Continue proven secondary prevention irrespective of the beta-blocker decision. Explain that absence of demonstrated routine benefit in one population is not evidence that the drug has no role in coronary care. questions.question: A patient with ACS has hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL without active bleeding. The team is reviewing the 2025 ACC/AHA recommendation and MINT evidence. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The nonsignificant MINT result establishes equivalent safety of restrictive and liberal strategies
A seven-gram threshold remains the preferred ACS default because restrictive trials in other inpatients apply directly
MINT proved a statistically significant reduction in its primary endpoint with liberal transfusion
A liberal transfusion strategy toward hemoglobin around ten may be reasonable, with individualized benefit–risk assessment
questions.explanation:
Transfusion Strategy in ACS With Anemia

Correct answer: A liberal transfusion strategy toward hemoglobin around ten may be reasonable, with individualized benefit–risk assessment

Read the Trial Result Without Converting Uncertainty Into Equivalence

**MINT compared restrictive and liberal transfusion strategies in MI with hemoglobin below ten.** Thirty-day death or MI occurred in 16.9% versus 14.5%, respectively.

The modeled relative risk for restrictive versus liberal treatment was 1.15, with a ninety-five-percent confidence interval of 0.99–1.34 and P=0.07.

This did not establish statistical superiority of the liberal strategy, but clinically important harm from a restrictive strategy could not be excluded. A nonsignificant result does not prove the strategies equivalent.

Apply the Recommendation to the Actual Patient

**The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline states that transfusion to achieve hemoglobin at least ten may be reasonable in ACS with anemia.** This is a qualified recommendation rather than a universal mandate.

Consider continuing ischemia, symptoms, anemia trajectory, heart failure, renal function and transfusion-associated circulatory overload. Reassess after each transfusion step according to clinical practice.

Investigate the cause of anemia and distinguish this nonbleeding presentation from active major hemorrhage, where resuscitation and source control have their own urgency. Review antithrombotic exposure and occult blood loss. Do not replace the measured clinical course with a single threshold detached from context, and do not extrapolate these ACS findings to every stable medical inpatient. Explain the expected benefit and uncertainty while monitoring for adverse transfusion effects. The question tests appropriate interpretation and individualized management, not certainty that one hemoglobin target is optimal for every patient.

The nonsignificant MINT result establishes equivalent safety of restrictive and liberal strategies: A superiority comparison with P=0.07 does not establish equivalence; its confidence interval still permits clinically important harm from the restrictive strategy.

A seven-gram threshold remains the preferred ACS default because restrictive trials in other inpatients apply directly: Restrictive thresholds are supported in several other settings, but ACS-specific evidence and the named recommendation warrant separate interpretation rather than direct extrapolation.

MINT proved a statistically significant reduction in its primary endpoint with liberal transfusion: The primary comparison favored liberal treatment numerically but did not reach conventional statistical significance; overstating certainty misrepresents the trial.

MINT randomized transfusion trial, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307983

ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI ACS guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009

questions.question: Nine months after drug-eluting stent implantation, a patient develops recurrent exertional angina despite antianginal treatment. Angiography shows focal severe in-stent restenosis with preserved flow and no acute thrombotic occlusion. Before selecting repeat PCI treatment, which assessment is most useful?
options: Repeat coronary calcium scoring to characterize the stented segment
Platelet-function testing to determine the cause of the focal narrowing
Intracoronary IVUS or OCT to define underexpansion, tissue growth and other mechanisms
Repeat exercise ECG to distinguish neointimal hyperplasia from underexpansion
questions.explanation:
Investigating the Mechanism of Coronary Stent Failure

Correct answer: Intracoronary IVUS or OCT to define underexpansion, tissue growth and other mechanisms

Identify the Structural Cause Before Reintervening

**IVUS or OCT helps establish the mechanism of stent failure.** The 2023 SCAI consensus emphasizes imaging because angiography alone provides incomplete information about the stent and surrounding tissue.

Underexpansion, neointimal hyperplasia, neoatherosclerosis and fracture can require different lesion preparation and treatment. Placing another stent without addressing the cause can perpetuate failure.

Select the imaging technique according to the anatomical question, renal function, contrast requirements and expertise. This is structural intravascular imaging, distinct from FFR assessment of physiological lesion significance.

Separate Restenosis From Acute Thrombotic Failure

**Stent thrombosis usually presents as an ACS and requires urgent coronary assessment and reperfusion.** Once flow is restored, investigate mechanical and medication-related contributors.

Restenosis commonly produces recurrent angina but can also present as ACS. Time since implantation and symptoms alone therefore cannot establish or exclude thrombosis.

For symptomatic restenosis, image-guided correction and an appropriate drug-coated balloon or repeat drug-eluting stent strategy depend on mechanism, prior layers and anatomy. Recurrent diffuse failure can warrant Heart Team discussion of surgery. Review adherence and secondary prevention in parallel; increasing antiplatelet intensity alone does not correct fixed mechanical underexpansion.

Repeat coronary calcium scoring to characterize the stented segment: Calcium scoring can inform atherosclerotic risk in other settings but cannot reliably identify the intrastent mechanism needed to plan this repeat intervention.

Platelet-function testing to determine the cause of the focal narrowing: Selected platelet testing can address antiplatelet response, especially in thrombotic presentations, but does not distinguish mechanical underexpansion from neointimal tissue causing this restenosis.

Repeat exercise ECG to distinguish neointimal hyperplasia from underexpansion: Exercise testing can demonstrate ischemia in suitable patients but cannot identify the structural cause of a known focal intrastent lesion.

ESC chronic coronary syndromes guideline, 2024 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehae177

questions.topic: Chronic coronary disease angina and landmark evidence
questions.question: A patient with stable exertional angina has sinus rate 49/min, blood pressure 158/86 mm Hg and LVEF 60%. There is no recent MI or other indication for rate slowing. Which initial antianginal is best suited among these choices?
options: Amlodipine
Metoprolol
Diltiazem
Verapamil
questions.explanation:
Antianginal Selection With Bradycardia and Hypertension

Correct answer: Amlodipine

Match the Drug to Heart Rate and Blood Pressure

**Amlodipine provides arterial vasodilation without clinically important direct sinus or AV-nodal suppression.** It can address both angina and the elevated pressure in this patient.

Beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium antagonists are useful antianginals in appropriate patients, but their rate-slowing effects matter when the resting pulse is already low.

Evaluate symptomatic bradycardia, conduction disease and medication causes separately. Choosing an antianginal does not remove the need to understand an unexpectedly slow pulse.

Separate Symptom Control From Prognostic Therapy

**Antianginal treatment is individualized according to hemodynamics, ventricular function and comorbidity.** No single first-line drug is optimal for every stable coronary presentation.

Amlodipine commonly starts at ==5 mg once daily==, with lower initiation in selected frail patients and titration to ==10 mg once daily== according to response. Monitor edema, dizziness and hypotension.

Avoid casually combining a beta blocker with verapamil or diltiazem because bradycardia and AV block can be amplified. Nondihydropyridines are also unsuitable in significant systolic dysfunction. If blood pressure were low as well as heart rate, a hemodynamically neutral option such as ranolazine might be more attractive after interaction screening. Continue lipid lowering and other indicated secondary prevention independently of symptom treatment. Persistent lifestyle-limiting angina despite suitable therapy warrants reassessment of ischemia and anatomy rather than unstructured escalation of drugs that worsen the patient’s physiological constraints.

Metoprolol: Metoprolol reduces angina through rate and contractility effects and is useful when tachycardia or another indication exists; this patient already has substantial resting bradycardia.

Diltiazem: Diltiazem can treat angina and hypertension, but its nodal effects may further slow the heart rate; a dihydropyridine better matches the current physiology.

Verapamil: Verapamil is an antianginal rate-slowing calcium antagonist, but resting bradycardia makes its chronotropic and conduction effects less suitable here.

questions.question: A patient with chronic angina is taking diltiazem. Ranolazine extended release is being considered after review of renal function, ECG and other drugs. Under the US prescribing information, what is the maximum ranolazine dose while diltiazem continues?
options: 500 mg twice daily
1000 mg twice daily
750 mg twice daily
375 mg twice daily
questions.explanation:
Ranolazine With Concurrent Diltiazem

Correct answer: 500 mg twice daily

Identify the Pharmacokinetic Interaction

**Diltiazem is a moderate CYP3A inhibitor and increases ranolazine exposure.** The US prescribing information limits ranolazine to ==500 mg twice daily== during this combination.

The ordinary extended-release regimen starts at five hundred milligrams twice daily and may increase to one thousand twice daily when suitable; the interacting-drug limit overrides that usual ceiling.

Strong CYP3A inhibitors and CYP3A inducers are contraindicated combinations rather than situations managed simply by the same dose cap.

Screen Beyond Heart Rate and Blood Pressure

**Ranolazine inhibits late inward sodium current and can improve angina with relatively little effect on resting pulse or pressure.** Hemodynamic neutrality does not imply freedom from important adverse effects.

It can prolong QT in an exposure-dependent manner. Review baseline QT, other QT-prolonging medicines, electrolytes, renal function and liver disease; liver cirrhosis is a labeled contraindication.

Dizziness, constipation and nausea can limit treatment. Monitor renal function, particularly with impairment or an acute illness, and review interactions involving other substrates as well as inhibitors. Extended-release tablets should be taken according to the formulation instructions rather than crushed or converted into an improvised dosing schedule. The drug treats chronic symptoms and does not replace acute reperfusion, antiplatelet treatment or lipid lowering when those are indicated. If angina remains limiting at the safe tolerated dose, reassess the regimen and coronary mechanism rather than exceeding an interaction-based ceiling.

1000 mg twice daily: This is the usual maximum without a relevant interacting inhibitor, but diltiazem increases ranolazine exposure and lowers the permitted maximum.

750 mg twice daily: Seven hundred fifty milligrams twice daily is a usual maximum in some European product information, but the question specifies the US prescribing information and its diltiazem interaction ceiling.

375 mg twice daily: Three hundred seventy-five milligrams twice daily is a starting dose in some European formulations; it is not the specified US maximum during moderate CYP3A inhibition.

questions.question: A patient with stable coronary disease has lifestyle-limiting angina despite tolerated guideline-directed therapy. A significant focal stenosis matches the ischemic territory and is suitable for PCI. LVEF is normal and left-main disease is absent. What is the best explanation for offering PCI?
options: PCI is offered primarily for an established survival advantage in this focal normal-EF presentation
PCI is recommended to improve persistent symptoms, without promising a universal survival benefit in this setting
PCI should await development of LV dysfunction before symptoms justify intervention
PCI should be reserved for a future ACS because symptoms alone do not justify it
questions.explanation:
Symptom-Driven Revascularization in Stable Coronary Disease

Correct answer: PCI is recommended to improve persistent symptoms, without promising a universal survival benefit in this setting

Define the Intended Benefit Before Recommending a Procedure

**Revascularization is recommended for lifestyle-limiting angina despite appropriate therapy when significant disease is amenable to treatment.** Symptom relief and improved daily function are meaningful outcomes.

Confirm that the lesion is clinically relevant rather than assuming every angiographic narrowing causes the reported symptoms.

Discuss procedural risks, bleeding and antiplatelet requirements, expected symptom benefit and the possibility of persistent symptoms from another mechanism.

Keep Prognostic Indications Population-Specific

**Selected anatomy and ventricular dysfunction can create a separate survival indication**, particularly when CABG is appropriate for significant left-main disease or multivessel disease with severe LV dysfunction.

Do not transfer CABG survival evidence automatically to PCI or extend stable-disease trial results to excluded high-risk anatomy.

A Heart Team assessment is useful for complex multivessel disease or uncertainty about the preferred method. Continue lipid lowering, lifestyle treatment and other indicated prevention after intervention. If symptoms improve, reassess the need for antianginal drugs individually rather than assuming all coronary medicines can stop. The decision should reflect the patient’s symptom burden and preferences alongside anatomy and clinical risk. Accurate counseling neither dismisses symptom-directed PCI nor promises that treating one stable lesion necessarily prolongs life in every patient.

questions.topic: Chronic coronary disease angina and landmark evidence
questions.question: A stable patient has a seventy-percent unprotected left-main stenosis. A colleague cites ISCHEMIA as proof that an initial conservative strategy is equivalent for this anatomy. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Significant unprotected left-main disease was excluded, so the trial cannot justify that extrapolation
The overall neutral comparison supports medical therapy first for this left-main lesion
The conservative arm prohibited later angiography, limiting comparison with current practice
The lack of statistical significance establishes equivalence between strategies in stable CAD
questions.explanation:
Applying ISCHEMIA Beyond Its Enrollment Population

Correct answer: Significant unprotected left-main disease was excluded, so the trial cannot justify that extrapolation

Check Eligibility Before Applying a Trial Result

**ISCHEMIA enrolled selected stable patients with moderate or severe ischemia.** Significant unprotected left-main disease was excluded, so its initial-strategy comparison does not settle management of this patient.

Other major exclusions included EF below thirty-five percent, recent ACS, unacceptable angina despite maximally tolerated treatment and advanced kidney disease in the main trial.

The parallel ISCHEMIA-CKD study addressed a different kidney-disease population and must not be silently substituted for the main trial.

Distinguish Strategy, Symptoms and Prognosis

**An initial conservative strategy includes active medical treatment and later angiography when indicated.** It does not mean permanent prohibition of revascularization.

The November 2026 ISCHEMIA-EXTEND report found no significant all-cause survival difference over a median nine-year follow-up. Estimated eleven-year mortality was 25.8% with initial invasion versus 26.9% with initial conservative management; adjusted hazard ratio 0.97, ninety-five-percent confidence interval 0.86–1.09. This survival analysis does not eliminate symptom benefits or extend eligibility to excluded patients.

Significant left-main disease requires anatomy-based specialist assessment and consideration of revascularization, often through a Heart Team. The suitable method depends on complexity, operative risk and other patient factors. Do not use a nonsignificant overall trial comparison to claim formal equivalence in an excluded subgroup. Similarly, severe uncontrolled symptoms remain a clinical indication for reassessment even when a patient otherwise resembles trial participants. The central examination skill is external validity: identify who was randomized, which strategies were compared and which conclusion the data can actually support.

The overall neutral comparison supports medical therapy first for this left-main lesion: An overall result applies within the population and strategies studied; it cannot establish a conservative-first conclusion for significant left-main disease that the trial excluded.

The conservative arm prohibited later angiography, limiting comparison with current practice: The conservative strategy allowed angiography and revascularization for clinical indications; the relevant limitation here is excluded anatomy rather than a permanent ban on invasive care.

The lack of statistical significance establishes equivalence between strategies in stable CAD: Failure to demonstrate superiority does not establish formal equivalence, and neither interpretation can extend the randomized comparison to this excluded anatomical subgroup.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the original FAME and COURAGE randomized trials?
options: FAME compared FFR-selected PCI with medical therapy; COURAGE compared PCI with CABG
FAME compared PCI with medical therapy alone; COURAGE compared physiological with angiographic PCI guidance
FAME compared physiological versus angiographic PCI guidance; COURAGE compared initial PCI plus medical therapy with medical therapy alone
FAME compared FFR-guided with angiographic PCI; COURAGE compared intensive with moderate lipid lowering
questions.explanation:
FAME and COURAGE Answer Different Questions

Correct answer: FAME compared physiological versus angiographic PCI guidance; COURAGE compared initial PCI plus medical therapy with medical therapy alone

Identify the Randomized Comparison

**Original FAME tested FFR-guided versus angiography-guided multivessel PCI.** In the physiological arm, lesions were treated when FFR was at most 0.80.

At one year, the composite of death, MI or repeat revascularization was 13.2% with FFR guidance versus 18.3% with angiographic guidance. This is a composite strategy result, not proof of isolated mortality benefit.

Do not confuse original FAME with FAME 2, which addressed a different comparison involving FFR-selected PCI and medical therapy.

Interpret Medical-Therapy Evidence Without Abandoning Symptom Care

**COURAGE compared initial PCI plus optimal medical therapy with optimal medical therapy alone in selected stable coronary disease.** It did not demonstrate a reduction in death or nonfatal MI from adding initial PCI.

Medical therapy in both arms was active preventive and antianginal treatment. A conservative initial strategy did not prohibit later revascularization when clinically required.

FFR reflects the pressure consequence of an epicardial lesion during hyperemia; it is not a test that excludes every microvascular or vasospastic mechanism of angina. Interpret borderline measurements and acute-infarct physiology with appropriate clinical caution. Use the trials to clarify whether a patient needs revascularization and, separately, which lesions should be treated. Their results do not negate symptom-directed intervention or anatomy-specific prognostic indications outside the studied comparison. Knowing the trial name is less useful than identifying its population, comparator and endpoint.

FAME compared FFR-selected PCI with medical therapy; COURAGE compared PCI with CABG: The first comparison resembles FAME 2 rather than original FAME; COURAGE compared adding PCI to medical therapy and did not randomize patients between PCI and CABG.

FAME compared PCI with medical therapy alone; COURAGE compared physiological with angiographic PCI guidance: These trial designs are reversed: original FAME studied how to select lesions during planned multivessel PCI, whereas COURAGE studied adding initial PCI to medical therapy.

FAME compared FFR-guided with angiographic PCI; COURAGE compared intensive with moderate lipid lowering: The FAME description is correct, but COURAGE randomized the initial PCI strategy on a background of optimal medical therapy, not statin intensity as its assigned intervention.

COURAGE randomized trial, 2007 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa070829

FAME randomized trial, 2009 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0807611

AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.04.003

questions.question: A patient has recurrent nocturnal rest angina with transient ST elevation. Coronary functional testing confirms epicardial spasm without a flow-limiting fixed lesion. Heart rate is 76/min, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg and EF is normal. Which preventive treatment is preferred?
options: A beta blocker alone as the principal antispasm treatment
A calcium channel blocker titrated to suppress episodes
Ranolazine alone before attempting calcium channel blockade
A long-acting nitrate as initial preventive monotherapy before calcium channel blockade
questions.explanation:
Preventing Recurrent Epicardial Coronary Spasm

Correct answer: A calcium channel blocker titrated to suppress episodes

Treat Dynamic Vasoconstriction

**Calcium channel blockers are first-line preventive therapy for confirmed vasospastic angina.** They reduce coronary smooth-muscle contraction and help prevent recurrent ischemic episodes.

Select a dihydropyridine or nondihydropyridine according to pulse, blood pressure, conduction and ventricular function. For example, amlodipine is prescribed at ==5–10 mg once daily== for vasospastic angina, starting at the lower end and titrating to response. Monitor pressure, edema and dizziness; hepatic impairment and frailty can warrant more cautious initiation.

Short-acting nitrates relieve episodes when suitable. Long-acting nitrates can be added for recurrent symptoms, with dosing designed to limit tolerance and with PDE5 interaction screening.

Address Triggers and Overlapping Coronary Disease

**Smoking cessation and avoidance of provoking vasoconstrictors are important.** Review cocaine or stimulant exposure and medicines that may precipitate spasm.

Spasm can coexist with atherosclerosis or microvascular dysfunction, so preventive treatment and additional antianginal choices should reflect the demonstrated mechanisms.

A nondiagnostic resting ECG between episodes does not exclude the condition. Persistent pain or prolonged ST elevation requires emergency assessment for occlusion and infarction. Refractory episodes, syncope or ventricular arrhythmia warrant specialist evaluation and treatment intensification. Suppression of pain does not eliminate every arrhythmic risk. Calcium antagonism is the initial preventive step, with adjuncts and follow-up based on response.

A beta blocker alone as the principal antispasm treatment: Beta blockers are useful for demand-related angina and other indications, but are not the preferred treatment for isolated epicardial spasm and may aggravate vasoconstriction in susceptible patients.

Ranolazine alone before attempting calcium channel blockade: Ranolazine can help selected chronic angina patients, but confirmed spasm has a more directly supported first-line calcium antagonist strategy.

A long-acting nitrate as initial preventive monotherapy before calcium channel blockade: Long-acting nitrates can be added for recurrent spasm despite calcium antagonism or selected when alternatives are unsuitable, but calcium channel blockade is the preferred initial preventive approach in this eligible patient.

questions.question: A patient has exertional angina and objective ischemia without obstructive epicardial disease. Coronary function testing shows Doppler-derived CFR 1.8 and IMR 32 units, without provoked spasm. Which management principle is appropriate?
options: Select a vasospasm-directed regimen without using the resistance and provocation findings
Reassure that the absence of an obstructive angiographic lesion excludes a coronary cause
Treat the demonstrated microvascular dysfunction with individualized antianginal and risk-factor therapy
Perform empiric PCI of the vessel with the lowest flow reserve despite no focal obstruction
questions.explanation:
Mechanism-Based Treatment of Microvascular Angina

Correct answer: Treat the demonstrated microvascular dysfunction with individualized antianginal and risk-factor therapy

Interpret the Functional Measurements Together

**Reduced coronary flow reserve and increased microvascular resistance support coronary microvascular dysfunction.** A nonobstructive angiogram does not make objective ischemia noncardiac.

Flow reserve integrates resting and hyperemic flow. The 2024 ESC guideline identifies Doppler CFR below 2.5 as abnormal in nonobstructive disease; IMR at least 25 units indicates increased microvascular resistance. CFR thresholds vary with method and framework, commonly below 2.0–2.5, so report the technique instead of treating one cutoff as universal.

Acetylcholine testing addresses spasm and endothelial responses; a different positive endotype can change the preferred treatment. Avoid assigning every patient the same mechanism from symptoms alone.

Tailor Treatment to the Demonstrated Endotype

**Antianginal selection should account for the microvascular mechanism, heart rate, blood pressure and comorbidity.** Beta blockers, calcium antagonists or ranolazine may be useful in selected reduced-reserve or increased-resistance presentations.

Calcium antagonists are preferred when epicardial or microvascular spasm is demonstrated. Overlapping endotypes may require combination treatment.

Address hypertension, lipids, smoking, physical conditioning and metabolic risk; ACE inhibition or other treatment should be selected according to the clinical context. Symptom improvement does not establish an identical mortality effect for every endotype-directed drug. Reassess symptoms and tolerability, and consider additional noncoronary contributors without dismissing documented coronary dysfunction.

Mechanism-Based Treatment of Microvascular Angina

Correct answer: C — Treat the demonstrated microvascular dysfunction with individualized antianginal and risk-factor therapy

Interpret the Functional Measurements Together

  • Reduced coronary flow reserve and increased microvascular resistance support coronary microvascular dysfunction. A nonobstructive angiogram does not make objective ischemia noncardiac.
    • Flow reserve integrates resting and hyperemic flow. The 2024 ESC guideline identifies Doppler CFR below 2.5 as abnormal in nonobstructive disease; IMR at least 25 units indicates increased microvascular resistance. CFR thresholds vary with method and framework, commonly below 2.0–2.5, so report the technique instead of treating one cutoff as universal.
    • Acetylcholine testing addresses spasm and endothelial responses; a different positive endotype can change the preferred treatment. Avoid assigning every patient the same mechanism from symptoms alone.

Tailor Treatment to the Demonstrated Endotype

  • Antianginal selection should account for the microvascular mechanism, heart rate, blood pressure and comorbidity. Beta blockers, calcium antagonists or ranolazine may be useful in selected reduced-reserve or increased-resistance presentations.
    • Calcium antagonists are preferred when epicardial or microvascular spasm is demonstrated. Overlapping endotypes may require combination treatment.
    • Address hypertension, lipids, smoking, physical conditioning and metabolic risk; ACE inhibition or other treatment should be selected according to the clinical context. questions.question: A patient with stable coronary and peripheral arterial disease has high recurrent ischemic risk, low bleeding risk, adequate renal function and no indication for DAPT or therapeutic anticoagulation. Which regimen is an evidence-supported option for intensifying long-term prevention?
options: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin
Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily plus low-dose aspirin
Rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily without aspirin
Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus clopidogrel
questions.explanation:
Selected Long-Term Dual-Pathway Inhibition

Correct answer: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus low-dose aspirin

Select Patients Before Intensifying Antithrombotic Treatment

**Low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin is an option in selected high-ischemic-risk chronic coronary disease without high bleeding risk.** The 2023 AHA/ACC framework specifies no separate need for therapeutic DOAC dosing or DAPT.

The vascular dose is ==2.5 mg twice daily== with low-dose aspirin. It must not be substituted for therapeutic anticoagulation when AF or venous thromboembolism requires it.

Review bleeding history, renal and hepatic function, stroke history, interactions and adherence. Polyvascular disease increases ischemic risk but does not erase bleeding contraindications.

Explain the COMPASS Benefit and Harm Together

**COMPASS showed fewer cardiovascular deaths, strokes or MIs with the combination than with aspirin alone.** Primary events occurred in 4.1% versus 5.4%, with hazard ratio 0.76.

Major bleeding increased: 3.1% versus 1.9%, with hazard ratio 1.70. The result supports patient selection rather than universal intensification.

Continue lipid lowering, smoking cessation, blood-pressure management and exercise-based care; antithrombotic escalation does not replace these interventions. Reassess the regimen if bleeding, renal deterioration or a new anticoagulation indication develops. Extended DAPT in selected prior-MI patients is a different strategy with its own evidence and eligibility, not a reason to combine every available agent. Discuss both expected ischemic benefit and bleeding burden so the chosen prescription reflects the individual patient’s risk and preferences.

Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily plus low-dose aspirin: Therapeutic-dose rivaroxaban has other indications such as eligible AF stroke prevention; it is not the COMPASS low-dose combination strategy requested here.

Rivaroxaban 5 mg twice daily without aspirin: This rivaroxaban-alone arm was studied in COMPASS but did not establish the same benefit as low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin; the successful combination cannot be replaced by this higher-dose monotherapy.

Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus clopidogrel: Clopidogrel is appropriate in several coronary and peripheral-arterial contexts, but substituting it for aspirin does not reproduce the COMPASS randomized combination evidence tested by this question.

COMPASS randomized trial, 2017 — https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1709118

AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.04.003
